{{神社 |名称 = 松峰神社 |画像 = [[File:Matumine Zinzya Honden.jpg|250px]] |所在地 = [[秋田県]][[大館市]]松峰字大山外 | 緯度度 = 40 | 緯度分 = 18 | 緯度秒 = 52.6 | N(北緯)及びS(南緯) = N | 経度度 = 140 |経度分 = 31 | 経度秒 = 50.6 | E(東経)及びW(西経) = E | 地図国コード = JP |地図=Japan Akita |祭神 = [[ツクヨミ]] |社格 = 村社 |創建 = [[817年]]（弘仁8年） |本殿 = |別名 = |札所等 = |例祭 = |神事 = }} '''松峰山信仰遺跡群'''（まつみねさんしんこういせきぐん）は、[[秋田県]][[大館市]]松峰字大山10にある松峰神社を中心にして、[[古代]]・[[中世]]に縁起を持つ[[密教]]関連[[遺跡]]である。松峰山は本尊の松峰不動明王にちなんだ名称で、中央にある山は標高375.7mの大山である。大館市松峰字仁王田141-5にある里宮は今は松峰[[稲荷神社]]になっている。松峰山信仰遺跡群は[[2009年]]（平成21年）5月1日に大館市指定[[史跡]]に指定された（地図の座標は、文化財指定された際の位置図より）。[[江戸時代]]には大館八景の「松峰暮雪」として知られ、[[秋田六郡三十三観音霊場]]の32番霊場でもあった。 == 縁起 == 本尊：不動明王（伝弘法大師作） 、前立二童子 末社：薬師堂、山の神、宇賀神社、倶利伽羅不動滝（この滝の下は祓川となっている）、岩谷十一面観音（伝弘法大師作）、正観音（宣長作） [[817年]]（弘仁8年）に[[弘法大師]]がこの山を開基する。金銅で阿弥陀観音像を作って、白銀で鏡を作り大円光と名付ける。[[822年]]（弘仁13年）左大臣誠公社殿が造営される。[[857年]]（天安元年）3月、地震のために全てが埋没する。[[891年]]（寛平3年）宇多天皇は出羽郡司の[[小野良実]][[小野小町]]の父の子、小野良房を勅使として額を賜る。「いやましの光りも時に埋まるる あらはれ照らせ松峯の月」同年、月山大権現と書いた真筆の額を奉納する。895年（寛平7年）、小野良房を奉行として社殿を造成する。 以後、数百年の間経歴ははっきりしない。[[1403年]]（応永10年）、領主の[[浅利氏]]が社殿造成以後、同家の崇敬するところになる。慶安元年、[[佐竹氏]]が不動仏を信仰して、本社は仏堂の姿に変わる。寛政年間に別当の伝寿院の僧侶が土中より駅路の鈴を発見する。[[1801年]]（享和元年）藩主[[佐竹義和]]が領地巡検の際に、この鈴を献上する。明治3年不動仏を廃する。例祭には旧藩庁より弊物を送られる。[[1873年]]（明治6年）に村社になる。現在の祀神は月読大神である。本殿は昔、古田中村と称したが、鎮座する山名の松峰をとってその名とした『釈迦内郷土誌』、釈迦内公民館、p.93-95。 本殿の狛犬は、[[伊多波武助]]が奉納したものである『秋田ふしぎ探訪』、無明舎出版、1979年。 == 「出羽秋田郡比内庄松峯山縁起」 == 松峰山の縁起を記録した古書は数多くある。代表的なものは『秋田六郡三十三観音巡礼記』享保年間（1716年-1736年）、[{{NDLDC|1174121/16}} 秋田叢書第8巻収録]、『新秋田叢書』第3巻収録、『久保田郡邑記』[[1798年]](寛政10年)、近藤案左衛門、柴田次雄編著、無明舎出版、ISBN 4895443612、『秋田風土記』[[1815年]](文化12年)、淀川盛雛、『新秋田叢書』第15巻収録、『郷村史略』[[1858年]]（安政5年）頃修成、大館市史編さん資料第4集、石垣忠吉翻刻、『伊豆園茶話』『伊豆園茶話』10・15の巻、[[石井忠行]]、『新秋田叢書』第8巻、第9巻、『羽陰温古誌』明治16-36執筆、升尾旭水、『新秋田叢書』第三期13巻収録、「出羽秋田郡比内庄松峯山縁起」大正年間か？、新屋武三郎、『釈迦内郷土誌』、平成元年復刻、釈迦内公民館である。これらに記された内容は、誤写・誤記や筆者による加筆を除けば、原書は一冊であると考えられる。しかし、原書の所在は不明である。文章の内容から、原書の成立は[[1673年]]（寛文12年）から[[1687年]]（貞享4年）の間と想定できる。そして「出羽秋田郡比内庄松峯山縁起」が最も原書に近いものであるといえる『大館郷土博物館研究紀要 火内』第12号、2015年3月、p.13-29、「松峰山信仰遺跡群の資料」、大館市文化財保護審議会「松峰山信仰遺跡」検討小委員会。 *祓川 - 参道の石段下の向かって右にある不動の滝から流れる小川。不動の滝は参詣者の不浄を滝で洗い流す為にこの名がついている。（[[菅江真澄]]は「禊川」、「はらひ川」と記録している）（{{Coord|40|18|43.02|N|140|32|48.01|E|}}） *神明社 - 山のふもとから1町(100m程度)ほど進むと、右手の小さな丘に神明社の小祠がある。お伊勢様とも言う。（菅江真澄は「伊勢のうちとを斎る社」と記録している）（{{Coord|40|18|50.71|N|140|32|31.59|E|}}） *湯殿山 - 鼓岩を降りて左に回れば一の鳥居の下に出て、元の道路に到着する『釈迦内郷土誌』、釈迦内公民館、p.265-269、大正年間執筆 平成元年復刻。 == 三鈷鐃 == 三鈷鐃は松峰山中から出土した古鈴であり、江戸時代に佐竹氏に渡され、現在は[[東京国立博物館]]が所蔵している。佐竹氏から地元の別当の伝寿院への受け取り状の文面は残っており「出羽秋田郡比内庄松峯山縁起」にそれが記録されていて『羽陰温古誌』では「現にその証がある」としている。 地元では「駅路の鈴（鐸）（えきろのすず）」と呼ばれている。[[人見蕉雨]]は『秋の田草』で[[1797年]]（寛政9年）に、この地方を訪れた際に「松嶺の駅路の鈴も名のみ聞」と記している。続いて二階堂蜀島が[[1800年]]（寛政12年）にこの鈴を実見し「駅路鈴は…常州鹿島郡正等院に所蔵されている。または、この秋田比内郡の松嶺山の鈴でもある。これは100年前に谷中から掘り出されたもので、不動堂の神職が所蔵していたものの、何の為に使うのかが分からなかったものである。その後、西国から来た老人が、鹿島の鈴と大同小異だから『駅路の鈴』であることは間違いがないと言い、それが広がった」と記録している。 [[菅江真澄]]は[[1803年]]（享和3年）6月18日から22日ごろに、松峰山を訪ね、その様子を「贄能辞賀楽美」に記録している。「金蔵院の翁は93歳でなくなった。その翁が明応の頃に南沢の土砂崩れから駅路の鐸を掘り出した。明応（1492年-1501年）の頃である。家宝として8代所持していたが、近年佐竹氏に献上したと聞く」と書き、更にこれを駅路の鈴と呼んでいる点については、古くは鏡にもおびだまにも鈴を付けたという点を指摘し、駅路の鈴であるとする根拠が不足しているとして、そう呼ぶことに否定的であった。 この鈴の正体については「佐竹家所蔵の古鈴に就いて」『秋田県考古会誌』第三巻一号収録、佐々木兵一という論文もあるが、その正体に結論は下しかねている。この鈴は1999年（平成11年）4月24日から5月16日まで佐竹氏から移管され現在保管されている[[東京国立博物館]]より借用して「三鈷鐃里帰り展」が[[大館郷土博物館]]で開催された。 三鈷鐃は地震が原因で埋まったとされているが、『久保田郡邑記』『秋田風土記』『郷村史略』では、地震よって埋まった鉄鰐も一緒に掘り出されたという記録もみえる。 == 伝寿院 == 伝寿院は松峰山の別当として記録されている。伝は傳とも、寿は壽・授と記される例がある。[[菅江真澄]]は伝寿院の絵図を残していて、ふもとから見て一の鳥居の左に伝寿院を描いている。伝寿院は「釈迦内郷土誌」が書かれた頃には廃絶していた。 [[1598年]]に大館[[浅利氏]]が滅び、大館が[[秋田実季]]の支配地になったとき、伝寿院には合計70石の知行が秋田氏から与えられている。このことから、浅利氏時代あるいはその以前から松峰山は比内地方で広く信仰され、浅利氏とは直接関わらない存在であったと考えられる。江戸時代には大館佐竹家から9石、二人扶持が与えられていたことが諸資料にみえる。 == 不動堂 == 不動堂は松峰山の本殿である。[[1786年]]（天明6年）焼失したことが『久保田郡邑記』『秋田風土記』『郷村史略』に記録されている。 「諸色書留帳」という資料『大館地方資料文書』、大館市史編さん資料第16集収録によると、[[1863年]]（文久3年）4月8日の夜にも失火によって不動堂は焼失し、不動尊像も失われ、別当の伝寿院は大館佐竹家から謹慎50日を仰せつけられた。[[1867年]]（慶応3年）不動堂の再建が成った。材木は松峰山中から伐採し、近在近辺から寄進が呼びかけられた。しかし、[[1868年]]（慶応4年、明治元年）には[[秋田戦争]]があり、大館市街は焼き払われてしまい、さらに[[廃仏毀釈]]があったため、再建時には180両の寄進が集まったものの、[[1871年]]の不動堂遷宮のときには寄進は1両2分しか集まらず「不景気に相成り、どなたからも寄進が無い。誠にもってきのどく千万」（大館竹村家所蔵「永宝記」）という状況であった。 かつては[[真言宗]]松峰山という寺であったが、神仏分離により神社風に改修し、主神を月夜見命とし、名称を松峰神社と改めた。 == 薬師神社 == 薬師様、久須神社とも言われる。松峰神社本殿の左方の小高いところにある、1坪程度の社殿。堂の中には薬師如来像2体が奉納されている。正保丙戌年（[[1646年]]）と、宝暦十年（[[1760年]]）に奉納された仏像である。他に穴のあいた小石や「目」や「め」、「メ」と書いた品々が数多く奉納されている。階段の中頃の右に薬師の清水と言われる湧水があって、目を清めて目の健康を祈るのが通例になっている『松峰郷土誌』、松峰町内会刊 、[[1998年]]。 == 天狗様 == 松峰山には杉や松の数多くの巨木があったが、その巨木の中でもひときわ異彩を放つ巨木杉があってそれを村人は天狗杉と呼んだ。その杉の中は空洞で天狗の棲処と言われた。しかし、枯死したので大正6年に伐採され、伐根が松峰神社に伐木記念として奉納された。それから推測すると、直径3m近くの杉であったと思われる。太平洋戦争時には、特に飛行兵、飛行隊に入隊した兵の家族は天狗の葉団扇で自由に飛行する天狗のあやかって、白と赤のへらを奉納して祈願した。また、天狗の神通力から敵の弾丸から身を守ってくれると出征家庭からは良く参拝された。 == 水神社 == 石段手前の右にある、[[手水舎]]の奥にある小さな石祠。若水と言って、特定の時に特定の水を飲むと若返ると言い伝えられている。今でも、元旦と共に、若水を飲む風習が残っている。 == 御製 == 石段（{{Coord|40|18|52.32|N|140|31|51.85|E|}}）左方にある[[御製]]。秋田県には他に御製がある神社は無い。[[宇多天皇]]によるものである。（{{Coord|40|18|51.82|N|140|31|51.31|E|}}） == 稲荷神社 == 松峰神社の里宮が稲荷神社である。現在は松峰集落の西に位置している（{{Coord|40|18|25.3|N|140|32|47.27|E|}}）。 祭神は[[倉稲魂神]]、[[猿田彦]]、[[大宮売命]]の3神である。例祭は毎年10月10日に行われている。 境内には猿田彦の碑や、[[月待塔#二十三夜塔|二十三夜碑]]、馬頭観音と馬の石碑がある。 稲荷神社には、藁や茅で作られた3体のニンギョ様（人形様）がある。約450年の歴史があり、毎年11月の最終日曜、松峰集落でニンギョ様まつりが開催されている。およそ800年前[[源義経]]が、[[武蔵坊弁慶]]と[[那須与一]]を従えて当地方を通過したということで、松峰地区の人たちが畏敬の念をもって人形を作った。3体の人形の名前もそれぞれに彼らの名前が付いている。集落の3ヶ所の入り口に疫病や悪霊が入ってこないように人形を置いていたのが始まりである。大正の初め稲荷神社の境内に安置された「広報おおだて」、昭和61年4月16日号。 == 菅江真澄の記録と松峰山信仰遺跡群 == [[1803年]]（享和3年）6月、[[菅江真澄]]は松峰山を訪れ、それを「贄能辞賀楽美」に記録している。「4月8日は祀りがあって、本殿を参拝する人が多い。その昔はこの近くの優婆塞たちで、奈良の大嶺・葛城にまだ登っていない人々は『さんげさんげ』を唱えて、数珠・鈴繁・頭巾・ましこ・ひきしき・あやひ笠を身に装い。独鈷杖に法螺・錫杖を鳴らしてこの峰に入ったと言う」と記している。 == 山田敬三 == 大館市出身のマラソンランナーで、[[1953年]]の[[ボストンマラソン]]で世界最高記録で優勝した[[山田敬三]]は、若い頃、松峰神社の階段を上り下りして練習を行っていた大館市・釈迦内地域フィールドワーク　～松峰神社編～ [https://common3.pref.akita.lg.jp/genkimura/blog/?p=45876]。 == 松峰集落・松峰鉱山 == 松峰集落は大昔は田中村といい、釈迦内北西300m程度の下内川と花岡川の合流地点にあった。[[1963年]]に集落の真下の地下250-300m付近で約3000mtに及ぶ[[黒鉱]]鉱床が発見された。その採掘のため、地盤沈下が起こり、[[1976年]]までに85戸が現在地に集団移転した。[[1973年]]には付近に[[松峯駅]]が開業した。 松峰鉱山は大山鉱床を、オープンコラム工法という一種の露天掘りで採掘したもので、[[1932年]]の[[足尾銅山]]の年間記録を抜いて、[[1970年]]には年間16285tの日本記録を達成した。[[1979年]]には金属価格が高騰して、黒鉱比率を低減し、施設老朽化による保全のための出費にもかかわらず、22億8000万円の高収益を達成した。その後、金属価格の低迷のため、鉱量を残しながら[[1994年]]（平成6年）に松峰鉱山は閉山になった。 大正元間この地区は[[小坂鉱山]]や[[花岡鉱山]]の煙害が酷く、スモッグが覆った状態になった。被害は松峰地区が最も酷く、松峰山も大被害を受け、松や栗の木は全滅し、[[1915年]]（大正4年）には松峰山全部が伐採され、大々的な植林が行われた。松峰神社の階段脇の記念碑にもその経緯が詳細に記録されている。 == 大山 == {{Infobox 山 |名称 = 大山 |画像 = [[File:Ôyama(Ôdate si).jpg|250px]] |画像キャプション = 大館市 大山（松峰山） |標高 = 375.6 |座標 = {{coord|40|18|52.9|N|140|31|43.2|E|type:mountain_region:JP|display=inline}} |所在地 = {{JPN}}

'''Matumine Shrine''' ({{ill|Matumine Shrine|ja|松峰神社}}) is a Shinto shrine located in Matsumine, Oyamagai, Ōdate City, {{ill|Akita Prefecture|ja|秋田県}}.
'''Matumine-san Faith Sites''' ({{ill|Matumine-san Shinkō Iseki-gun|ja|松峰山信仰遺跡群}}) refers to the group of ancient and medieval esoteric ({{ill|Mikkyo|ja|密教}}) sites associated with auspicious legends that cluster around Matumine Shrine. The mountain, named after the honzon of the shrine—{{ill|Fudō Myōō|ja|不動明王|1=Acala|lt=Fudō Myōō|2=ja|3=不動明王}} of the former Ryouakkosan Dainenji—has its central peak, Ōyama, at an elevation of 375.7 m. The village shrine (satoyama) located at 141-5, Nioida, Ōdate City, is now known as the Matsumine {{ill|Inari Shrine|ja|稲荷神社}}. Matumine-san Faith Sites were designated as a historic site by Ōdate City on May 1, 2009 (Heisei 21), with coordinates based on the designated cultural property map. During the Edo period, it was known as "Matsumine Kureyuki" in the Eight Views of Ōdate and served as the 32nd sacred site in the Akita Rokugun Sanjū Sankannon Reijō.
== Legend == The honzon of Matumine Shrine is Fudō Myōō (attributed to the works of {{ill|Kōbō Daishi|ja|弘法大師}}) accompanied by two guardian child deities.
== Enshrined Deities and Subsidiary Shrines == * Honzon: Fudō Myōō (伝弘法大師作) and two guardian child deities (Zenritsu Nīdōji) * Subsidiary shrines include: Yakushidō, the mountain deity shrine, Uga Shrine, Kurikara Fudō Taki (whose waterfall becomes Haragawa), Iwaya Jūimen Kannon (attributed to Kōbō Daishi), and Shō Kannon (attributed to Senchō).
== History == In {{ill|817 AD|ja|817th year}} (Kōnin 8), {{ill|Kōbō Daishi|ja|弘法大師}} is said to have founded the mountain. He cast a bronze statue of Amida Kannon and made a mirror out of silver, naming it Daienkō. In {{ill|822 AD|ja|822nd year}} (Kōnin 13), the Left Minister Seikō-shaden was constructed. In March {{ill|857 AD|ja|857th year}} (Tennan 1), an earthquake buried all existing structures. In {{ill|891 AD|ja|891st year}} (Kanpei 3), Emperor Uda granted a headband to Ono Yoshimitsu, the son of Ono Yoshiya (father of Ono Komachi). That same year, a manuscript inscribed with “Yamashi no Hikari mo Toki ni Umamaruru, Araware Terase Matsumine no Tsuki” was presented. In {{ill|895 AD|ja|895th year}} (Kanpei 7), Ono Yoshifusa was appointed as the official, and the shrine building was constructed.
Afterwards, the subsequent history remains obscure for several centuries. In {{ill|1403 AD|ja|1403rd year}} (Ōei 10), the local lord of the {{ill|Asari clan|ja|浅利氏}} began to revere the shrine, and in the first year of Kei'an the Satake clan, devotees of Fudō, transformed the main shrine into a Buddhist temple hall. During the Kansei era, a monk from Denshūin discovered a bell in the soil. In {{ill|1801 AD|ja|1801st year}} (Kyōwa 1), the feudal lord Satake Yoshikazu presented this bell during a tour of his domain. In the 3rd year of the Meiji era, the Buddhist Fudō was abolished. For the regular festivals, items from the former domain were provided. In {{ill|1873 AD|ja|1873rd year}} (Meiji 6), the shrine was reclassified as a village shrine. The current enshrined deity is {{ill|Tsukuyomi|ja|月読大神}}. The main shrine building was formerly known as Furuta Nakamura, but it later adopted the name Matsumine Shrine, after the mountain on which it stands.<ref>『釈迦内郷土誌』, Shakani Kominkan, pp.93–95</ref>
The komainu at the main shrine were donated by {{ill|Itahabutakesuke|ja|伊多波武助}}.<ref>『秋田ふしぎ探訪』, Mumyōsha Publishing, 1979</ref>
== “Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi” == Numerous ancient texts record the legends of Matsumine-san. Representative texts include: * ''Akita Rokugun Sanjū Sankannon Junrei-ki''<ref>Kyōhō era (1716–1736), [{{NDLDC|1174121/16}}] in Akita Sōsho Vol.8 and in Shin Akita Sōsho Vol.3</ref> * ''Kubota-gun Eki-ki'' * ''Akita Fudoki'' * ''Gyōson Shiryaku'' * “Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi”<ref name="hinai">『大館郷土博物館研究紀要 火内』 Vol.12, March 2015, pp.13–29, “Materials on Matsumine-san Faith,” from the Matsumine-san Shinkō Iseki-gun Examination Subcommittee of the Ōdate City Cultural Property Protection Council</ref>
Other notable features on Matsumine-san include: * **Haragawa** – A small stream flowing from the waterfall of Fudō located on the right side below the stone steps of the approach. The waterfall is so named because it is used to wash away impurities from worshipers. ({{Coord|40|18|43.02|N|140|32|48.01|E|}}) * **Shinmeisha** – A small shrine on a hill about one chō (approximately 100 m) from the foot of the mountain; also called O-Ise-sama. ({{Coord|40|18|50.71|N|140|32|31.59|E|}}) * **Yuden-yama** – A distant monument to Yuden-yama, established in {{ill|1770 AD|ja|1770th year}}. ({{Coord|40|18|48.76|N|140|32|35.53|E|}}) * **Kōshin-zuka** – A mound established in {{ill|1778 AD|ja|1778th year}}. ({{Coord|40|18|48.61|N|140|32|34.72|E|}}) * **Okoishi and Obaishi** – Stones enshrining {{ill|Manjushri|ja|文殊菩薩}} and {{ill|Fugen Bosatsu|ja|普賢菩薩}}. ({{Coord|40|18|54.11|N|140|32|20.70|E|}}) and ({{Coord|40|18|54.73|N|140|32|19.62|E|}}) * **Yenaki Iwa** – A stone said to have the power to silence a crying child. ({{Coord|40|18|54.42|N|140|32|10.97|E|}}) * **Usa Shrine** – A small shrine near the first torii where a small grass sickle is offered to cure smallpox in children. ({{Coord|40|18|53.77|N|140|32|04.32|E|}}) * **The First Torii** – A large stone torii; historically, a pond and garden existed to its right. ({{Coord|40|18|54.02|N|140|31|59.77|E|}}) * **Denjuin** – As recorded by Sugae Masumi, an illustration depicts Denjuin to the left of the first torii. This structure once existed between the first torii and the former pond and is said to mark the beginning of the mountain climbing route.<ref name="meisyo">“Matsumine Mountain Scenic Tour Association” (record, June 16, Heisei 3) by the Matsumine Town Association</ref> * **Cedar Alley** – A row of giant cedars between the first torii and the main shrine building. Although not mentioned in Sugae Masumi’s writings, old maps clearly depict it. Currently, the largest cedar is approximately 6.5 m in circumference and is over 600 years old. ({{Coord|40|18|53.18|N|140|31|56.64|E|}}) * **Stone Steps** – Approximately 170 stone steps (commonly stated as 160), also known as “Ishinokizahashi.”<ref name="matu"/> * **Fudō-no-Taki** – The waterfall of Fudō on the right side of the stone steps, whose water flows from a sheer cliff and eventually becomes Haragawa. Worshipers use it for purification before ascending to the main shrine. ({{Coord|40|18|52.91|N|140|31|53.66|E|}}) * **Uga Shrine** – A small stone shrine located to the right, along the waterfall’s flow, known as Uga no Kami; it is also called the small water shrine of Uga. ({{Coord|40|18|52.91|N|140|31|53.66|E|}}) * **Main Shrine Building** – The shrine grounds cover an area of 6 tan 11 bu, and the current main building was constructed by Satake Yoshinori starting in Meiji 3 and completed in April of Meiji 4. ({{Coord|40|18|52.23|N|140|31|50.23|E|}}) * **Yakushidō** – Located to the upper left of the main shrine building, also known as Hisu Shrine; dedicated to Yakushi Nyorai. ({{Coord|40|18|51.39|N|140|31|50.11|E|}}) * **Yama Shrine** – A small shrine dedicated to the mountain deity located to the right of the main building; proceeding around it leads to the source of Fudō-no-Taki. ({{Coord|40|18|52.87|N|140|31|50.84|E|}}) * **Iwaya Jūimen Kannon** – From the middle of the Cedar Alley, a side path leads to a large rock cave at the foot of the mountain, enshrining the Eleven-Faced Kannon. ({{Coord|40|18|50.03|N|140|31|57.18|E|}}) * **Shiroiwa** – A sheer white rock cliff to the left of the cave. * **Tenjin no Iwa** – A rock on the northern peak where ancient pines and other trees grow, known as Tenjin Rock. * **Higashi Nozoki Iwa (Eastern Lookout Rock)** – A massive rock jutting out to provide a view of the eastern sky. ({{Coord|40|18|59.12|N|140|31|46.83|E|}}) * **Kagami Iwa** – A rock that stands like a mirror; also referred to as Eboshi Iwa, due to its unusual shape. ({{Coord|40|18|59.18|N|140|31|46.67|E|}}) * **Tainai Kugu (Inner Womb Cave)** – A cave-like opening in the rock, said to evoke the feeling of being within a mother’s womb. ({{Coord|40|18|59.08|N|140|31|46.21|E|}}) * **Hokoku Iwa** – Located north of Tainai Kugu near the resting area; recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Nozoki Iwa” or “Byōbu Iwa,” where a “nozoki shugyō” similar to that of Ōmine-san was practiced. ({{Coord|40|18|59.58|N|140|31|43.35|E|}}) * **Kyūjō** – Near the summit, a slightly flat resting area where a triangular survey marker once stood. * **Kineiwa** – To the west of the resting area, a rock resembling a mortar carried by a moon rabbit. (Currently obscured by trees; on the western slope.) * **Okunoin** – Stairs on the western side of the resting area leading to an inner sanctuary called Okunoin (recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Oku no Goza”). From here, ancient features such as the Goma steps, a Zazen stone, and the rock of Gongen were once noted, though they are no longer identifiable. * **Suzuri Iwa** – Descending from the summit toward the south, a rock with a concave bottom that always contains water, known as Kōbō’s inkstone. (Near Ōiwa on a neighboring southeastern peak; now obscured by vegetation.) * **Kengami Mine** – A sharp rock outcrop with little foothold, described by Sugae Masumi as “Kengamine.” ({{Coord|40|18|42.71|N|140|31|49.76|E|}}) * **Tengu Iwa** – The large rocks on Kengami Mine are called Tengu Rock, with the larger one known as Great Tengu and the smaller as Little Tengu. (As recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Daitengu, Shōtengu no Iwa”.) * **Hasami Iwa** – Rocks facing each other resembling scissors; encountered along a small, relatively flat path obstructed by a large rock. ({{Coord|40|18|39.93|N|140|31|49.45|E|}}) * **Tengu-bashi** – Also known as the Tengu Suspension Bridge, it is the most scenic spot on the mountain. A massive rock bridges a deep chasm; crossing it offers a daunting view below. (Recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Daitengu no Tsuri-bashi.”) ({{Coord|40|18|37.95|N|140|31|51.35|E|}}) * **Tsuzumi Iwa** – A flat rock encountered when descending from Tengu Iwa, which produces a drum-like sound when stepped upon. (Recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Kago Iwa” and also as Tsuzumi Iwa.) ({{Coord|40|18|34.86|N|140|31|51.11|E|}}) After descending from Tsuzumi Iwa and turning left, one emerges below the First Torii and reaches the original road.<ref>『釈迦内郷土誌』, Shakani Kominkan, pp.265–269, composed during the Taishō era and reprinted in Heisei 1.</ref> == Sankokuga (Three-hooked Bell) == Sankokuga is an ancient bell excavated from Matsumine-san, which was presented to the Satake clan during the Edo period and is now housed in the {{ill|Tokyo National Museum|ja|東京国立博物館}}. A receipt document from the Satake clan is recorded in the "Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi," and the "Hu Yin Onko-shi" confirms its existence. Locally, it is known as the "Station Bell" (Ekiro no Suzu). When [[Hitomi Shōu]] visited the region in 1797 (Kansei 9), he remarked that he had only heard of the Station Bell, and later Nikaidō Shokushima, in 1800 (Kansei 12), witnessed it and noted that it was housed at Seitōin in Kashima District or belonged to Matsumine-san in Dewa Akita-gun. He mentioned that it was unearthed in Tanaka about 100 years ago, and an elderly man from western regions confirmed that it was essentially identical to the bell from Kashima, hence the name "Station Bell" became established.<ref name="hinai"/> There is also a scholarly paper titled "On the Ancient Bell Housed by the Satake Family" discussing its true nature, though no definitive conclusion has been reached. This bell was transferred from the Satake family between April 24 and May 16, 1999 (Heisei 11) to the Tokyo National Museum, and was exhibited in the "Sankokuga Homecoming Exhibition" at the Ōdate Local Museum. According to some records in the "Kubota-gun Eki-ki," "Akita Fudoki," and "Gyōson Shiryaku," the bell was buried due to an earthquake, and an iron alligator was also excavated alongside it.<ref name="hinai"/> == Denjuin == Denjuin is recorded as the local temple of Matsumine-san. Sugae Masumi left an illustration of Denjuin, depicting it to the left of the First Torii when viewed from the base of the mountain. By the time the "Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi" was compiled, Denjuin had already been abolished. In {{ill|1598 AD|ja|1598th year}}, when the Asari clan perished and Ōdate came under the control of Akita Miki, Denjuin received a total of 70 shaku from the Akita clan. This indicates that Matsumine-san had been widely venerated in the Hinai region since the Asari era or earlier, independent of the Asari clan. During the Edo period, documents record that the Satake clan of Ōdate provided 9 shaku and two retinues.<ref name="hinai"/> == Fudō-dō == Fudō-dō is the main shrine building of Matsumine-san. According to records in the "Kubota-gun Eki-ki," "Akita Fudoki," and "Gyōson Shiryaku," it burned down in {{ill|1786 AD|ja|1786th year}} (Tenmei 6). According to a document titled "Shoshokurichū-chō," Fudō-dō also burned down on the night of April 8, 1863 (Bunkyū 3) due to a fire, resulting in the loss of the Fudō statue, and the local Denjuin was ordered by the Satake clan to observe 50 days of mourning. Fudō-dō was reconstructed in {{ill|1867 AD|ja|1867th year}} (Keiō 3). Timber was felled from within Matsumine-san, and contributions were solicited from the surrounding area. However, in 1868 (Keiō 4, Meiji 1), during the Akita War when Ōdate City was burned and amid the anti-Buddhist ({{ill|Haibutsu Kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈|1=Haibutsu kishaku}}) movement, although contributions of 180 ryo were collected at the time of reconstruction, by the time of the Fudō-dō relocation in 1871 only 1 ryo 2 bu was raised, indicating severe economic hardship.<ref name="hinai"/> Once a {{ill|Shingon sect|ja|真言宗}} temple known as Matsumine-san, it was later converted to a shrine in accordance with the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, with the principal deity changed to {{ill|Tsukuyomi|ja|月夜見命}}, and the name was changed to Matsumine Shrine. == Yakushi Shrine == Yakushi Shrine, also known as Hisu Shrine, is located on a small rise to the left of the main shrine building. It enshrines two statues of Yakushi Nyorai, which were donated in the Shōho Besshoku year (【1646 AD】) and in the Hōreki 10th year (【1760 AD】). In addition, many small stones with holes or inscribed with “me” are offered. A spring known as "Yakusui" is found midway up the steps; it is customary to purify one’s eyes with this water.<ref name="matu"/> == Tengu-sama == Among the many giant cedar and pine trees on Matsumine-san, one particularly distinctive giant cedar, known locally as the "Tengu Cedar," was reputed to have a hollow interior that served as the dwelling of tengu. However, as the tree died, it was cut down in Taishō 6, and the felled trunk was donated to Matsumine Shrine as a memorial. It is estimated to have had a diameter of nearly 3 m. During the Pacific War, families of soldiers—especially those whose relatives served in aviation units—visited the shrine and offered white and red paper fans in the hope of emulating the tengu’s ability to fly freely. It was also widely visited by families for protection against enemy bullets, due to the tengu’s reputed supernatural powers.<ref name="matu"/> == Suijin Shrine == Suijin Shrine is a small stone shrine located to the right, just before the stone steps. Known as Wakami, it is said that drinking water from here will restore youth; this tradition continues today on New Year’s Day.<ref name="matu"/> == Gosai == Gosai is a commemorative monument located to the left of the stone steps. There are no other monuments of its kind in Akita Prefecture. It is attributed to Emperor Uda. ({{Coord|40|18|51.82|N|140|31|51.31|E|}}) == Inari Shrine == The village shrine (satoyama) of Matsumine Shrine is an Inari Shrine, currently located in the western part of the Matsumine settlement ({{Coord|40|18|25.3|N|140|32|47.27|E|}}). Its enshrined deities are {{ill|Kura Inadama no Mikoto|ja|倉稲魂神}}, {{ill|Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦}}, and {{ill|Ōmiya-uru no Mikoto|ja|大宮売命}}. Its festival is held every October 10. Within its precincts there are monuments such as a stele of Sarutahiko, a “Twenty-Three Night Stele” (also known as Tsukimai-to), and a stone monument featuring a horse head.<ref name="matu"/> At the Inari Shrine, there are three dolls made of straw and pampas grass, with a history of approximately 450 years. Every last Sunday in November, the Matsumine settlement holds a doll festival. According to tradition, about 800 years ago, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitsune|ja|源義経}}, accompanied by {{ill|Musashibō Benkei|ja|武蔵坊弁慶}} and {{ill|Nasu no Yoichi|ja|那須与一}}, passed through this area, inspiring the local people to create dolls out of reverence. These dolls were originally placed at the three entrances to the settlement to ward off epidemics and evil spirits, and were later enshrined within the Inari Shrine during the early Taishō period.<ref>「広報おおだて」, Shōwa 61, April 16</ref> == Records by Sugae Masumi and the Matumine-san Faith Sites == In June 1803 (Kyōwa 3), Sugae Masumi visited Matsumine-san and recorded his impressions in "Nie Nō Jikagarami." He noted, "On April 8, when a ceremony is held, many people come to worship at the main shrine. In the old days, those local Upase people who had not yet ascended to Nara’s Ōmine or Katsuragi would chant 'sange sange' and adorn themselves with prayer beads, bells, headscarves, and ayahikasa, carrying a dango-staff along with a spiral staff and a scepter, as they entered this peak." == Yamada Keizō == Marathon runner Yamada Keizō, from Ōdate City, who won the Boston Marathon in 1953 with a world record time, practiced running up and down the stone steps of Matsumine Shrine in his youth.<ref>Ōdate City, “Shakani Fieldwork – Matsumine Shrine Edition” [https://common3.pref.akita.lg.jp/genkimura/blog/?p=45876]</ref> == Matsumine Settlement and Matsumine Mine == The Matsumine Settlement, formerly known as Tanaka Village, was located at the confluence of the Shimonakagawa and Hanaokagawa rivers, about 300 m from the village. In 1963, a black ore deposit extending approximately 3000 mt was discovered 250–300 m underground beneath the settlement. Due to mining, subsidence occurred, and by 1976, 85 households were collectively relocated to the present site. In 1973, Matsumine Station was opened in the vicinity. Matsumine Mine extracted black ore from the Ōyama ore deposit using an open-column (open-pit) method. In 1932, its annual output surpassed that of the Ashio Copper Mine, and in 1970 it achieved a national record of 16,285 t per year. In 1979, despite aging facilities and maintenance expenses, soaring metal prices led to high revenues of 2.28 billion yen. However, due to a downturn in metal prices, the mine was closed in 1994 (Heisei 6), while leaving some reserves intact. During the Taishō period, this area suffered from severe smog caused by emissions from Kosaka Mine and Hanaoka Mine; the Matsumine area was the worst affected. Matsumine-san suffered greatly, with all its pine and chestnut trees dying, and in 1915 (Taishō 4) the entire mountain was deforested, leading to extensive reforestation. The history of this event is detailed on a commemorative monument by the shrine's stone steps.<ref name="matu"/> == Ōyama == {{Infobox Mountain |Name = Ōyama |image = [[File:Ôyama(Ôdate si).jpg|250px]] |image Caption = Ōyama in Ōdate City (Matsumine-san) |Elevation = 375.6 m |Coordinates = {{coord|40|18|52.9|N|140|31|43.2|E|type:mountain_region:JP|display=inline}} |Location = {{JPN}}<br />{{ill|Akita Prefecture|ja|秋田県}}, {{ill|Ōdate City|ja|大館市}}, Matsumine Ōyama |Mountain Range = |Type = |First Ascent = |Map = {{Location map|Japan Akita Prefecture#Japan|relief=1|float=center}}{{日本の位置情報|40|18|53.05|140|31|43.2|Ōyama|40.314737,140.528669|Ōyama|nocoord=yes}} }} The highest peak of Matsumine-san is Ōyama (375.7 m), which epitomizes the very notion of a "mountain." On Ōyama, there is a pine known as the "Makka Pine," which, upon reaching 62 years of age, is said to be designated as such. Additionally, unusually for a mountain of roughly 300 m class, about 100 native {{ill|Buna|ja|ブナ}} trees grow here<ref name="matu"/>. Although the number of trees is small, Ōyama is home to many rare and endangered plant species, including {{ill|Urashima-sō|ja|ウラシマソウ}}, {{ill|Shōjōbakama|ja|ショウジョウバカマ}}, {{ill|Kuramayuri|ja|クルマユリ}}, {{ill|Iwanashi|ja|イワナシ}}, {{ill|Yamazaki-sō|ja|ヤマザキソウ}}, {{ill|Shunran|ja|シュンラン}}, {{ill|Kakiran|ja|カキラン}}, {{ill|Ginran|ja|ギンラン}}, {{ill|Ruiyōbotan|ja|ルイヨウボタン}}, {{ill|Jakōsō|ja|ジャコウソウ}}, {{ill|Kumokiriso|ja|クモキリソウ}}, {{ill|Jigabachisō|ja|ジガバチソウ}}, {{ill|Ginryōsō|ja|ギンリョウソウ}}, {{ill|Iwauchiwa|ja|イワウチワ}}, {{ill|Sasabaginran|ja|ササバギンラン}}, {{ill|Azumagiku|ja|アヅマギク}}, {{ill|Akabanamaru Bamanasaku|ja|アカバナマルバマンサク}}, and {{ill|Kumagaisho|ja|クマガイソウ}}, among others.<ref name="matu"/> At the summit of Ōyama stands the Ōdate Television Relay Station / Hanaya FM Relay. == Matsumine-san Faith Sites Image Gallery == <gallery> File:Matuminesan Kagamiiwa.jpg | Kagami Iwa File:Ôyama Santyô.jpg | The summit of Ōyama with television towers in the background File:Matumine Zinzya Iti no Torii.jpg | The first torii (an illustration by Sugae Masumi from a similar location) File:Matumine Iwaya Zyûitimen Kannon.jpg | Shrine for the Jūimen Kannon at Iwaya (the Kannon statue is no longer present) File:Matumine Inari Zinzya.jpg | Matsumine Shrine's village Inari Shrine </gallery> == Footnotes ==

'''Matumine Shrine''' ({{ill|Matumine Shrine|ja|松峰神社|12=draft}}) is a Shinto shrine located in Matsumine, Oyamagai, Ōdate City, {{ill|Akita Prefecture|ja|秋田県|12=draft}}.
'''Matumine-san Faith Sites''' ({{ill|Matumine-san Shinkō Iseki-gun|ja|松峰山信仰遺跡群|12=draft}}) refers to the group of ancient and medieval esoteric ({{ill|Mikkyo|ja|密教|12=draft}}) sites associated with auspicious legends that cluster around Matumine Shrine. The mountain, named after the honzon of the shrine—{{ill|Fudō Myōō|ja|不動明王|1=Acala|lt=Fudō Myōō|2=ja|3=不動明王|12=draft}} of the former Ryouakkosan Dainenji—has its central peak, Ōyama, at an elevation of 375.7 m. The village shrine (satoyama) located at 141-5, Nioida, Ōdate City, is now known as the Matsumine {{ill|Inari Shrine|ja|稲荷神社|12=draft}}. Matumine-san Faith Sites were designated as a historic site by Ōdate City on May 1, 2009 (Heisei 21), with coordinates based on the designated cultural property map. During the Edo period, it was known as "Matsumine Kureyuki" in the Eight Views of Ōdate and served as the 32nd sacred site in the Akita Rokugun Sanjū Sankannon Reijō.
== Legend == The honzon of Matumine Shrine is Fudō Myōō (attributed to the works of {{ill|Kōbō Daishi|ja|弘法大師|12=draft}}) accompanied by two guardian child deities.
== Enshrined Deities and Subsidiary Shrines == * Honzon: Fudō Myōō (伝弘法大師作) and two guardian child deities (Zenritsu Nīdōji) * Subsidiary shrines include: Yakushidō, the mountain deity shrine, Uga Shrine, Kurikara Fudō Taki (whose waterfall becomes Haragawa), Iwaya Jūimen Kannon (attributed to Kōbō Daishi), and Shō Kannon (attributed to Senchō).
== History == In {{ill|817 AD|ja|817th year|12=draft}} (Kōnin 8), {{ill|Kōbō Daishi|ja|弘法大師|12=draft}} is said to have founded the mountain. He cast a bronze statue of Amida Kannon and made a mirror out of silver, naming it Daienkō. In {{ill|822 AD|ja|822nd year|12=draft}} (Kōnin 13), the Left Minister Seikō-shaden was constructed. In March {{ill|857 AD|ja|857th year|12=draft}} (Tennan 1), an earthquake buried all existing structures. In {{ill|891 AD|ja|891st year|12=draft}} (Kanpei 3), Emperor Uda granted a headband to Ono Yoshimitsu, the son of Ono Yoshiya (father of Ono Komachi). That same year, a manuscript inscribed with “Yamashi no Hikari mo Toki ni Umamaruru, Araware Terase Matsumine no Tsuki” was presented. In {{ill|895 AD|ja|895th year|12=draft}} (Kanpei 7), Ono Yoshifusa was appointed as the official, and the shrine building was constructed.
Afterwards, the subsequent history remains obscure for several centuries. In {{ill|1403 AD|ja|1403rd year|12=draft}} (Ōei 10), the local lord of the {{ill|Asari clan|ja|浅利氏|12=draft}} began to revere the shrine, and in the first year of Kei'an the Satake clan, devotees of Fudō, transformed the main shrine into a Buddhist temple hall. During the Kansei era, a monk from Denshūin discovered a bell in the soil. In {{ill|1801 AD|ja|1801st year|12=draft}} (Kyōwa 1), the feudal lord Satake Yoshikazu presented this bell during a tour of his domain. In the 3rd year of the Meiji era, the Buddhist Fudō was abolished. For the regular festivals, items from the former domain were provided. In {{ill|1873 AD|ja|1873rd year|12=draft}} (Meiji 6), the shrine was reclassified as a village shrine. The current enshrined deity is {{ill|Tsukuyomi|ja|月読大神|12=draft}}. The main shrine building was formerly known as Furuta Nakamura, but it later adopted the name Matsumine Shrine, after the mountain on which it stands.<ref>『釈迦内郷土誌』, Shakani Kominkan, pp.93–95</ref>
The komainu at the main shrine were donated by {{ill|Itahabutakesuke|ja|伊多波武助|12=draft}}.<ref>『秋田ふしぎ探訪』, Mumyōsha Publishing, 1979</ref>
== “Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi” == Numerous ancient texts record the legends of Matsumine-san. Representative texts include: * ''Akita Rokugun Sanjū Sankannon Junrei-ki''<ref>Kyōhō era (1716–1736), [{{NDLDC|1174121/16}}] in Akita Sōsho Vol.8 and in Shin Akita Sōsho Vol.3</ref> * ''Kubota-gun Eki-ki'' * ''Akita Fudoki'' * ''Gyōson Shiryaku'' * “Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi”<ref name="hinai">『大館郷土博物館研究紀要 火内』 Vol.12, March 2015, pp.13–29, “Materials on Matsumine-san Faith,” from the Matsumine-san Shinkō Iseki-gun Examination Subcommittee of the Ōdate City Cultural Property Protection Council</ref>
Other notable features on Matsumine-san include: * **Haragawa** – A small stream flowing from the waterfall of Fudō located on the right side below the stone steps of the approach. The waterfall is so named because it is used to wash away impurities from worshipers. ({{Coord|40|18|43.02|N|140|32|48.01|E|}}) * **Shinmeisha** – A small shrine on a hill about one chō (approximately 100 m) from the foot of the mountain; also called O-Ise-sama. ({{Coord|40|18|50.71|N|140|32|31.59|E|}}) * **Yuden-yama** – A distant monument to Yuden-yama, established in {{ill|1770 AD|ja|1770th year|12=draft}}. ({{Coord|40|18|48.76|N|140|32|35.53|E|}}) * **Kōshin-zuka** – A mound established in {{ill|1778 AD|ja|1778th year|12=draft}}. ({{Coord|40|18|48.61|N|140|32|34.72|E|}}) * **Okoishi and Obaishi** – Stones enshrining {{ill|Manjushri|ja|文殊菩薩|12=draft}} and {{ill|Fugen Bosatsu|ja|普賢菩薩|12=draft}}. ({{Coord|40|18|54.11|N|140|32|20.70|E|}}) and ({{Coord|40|18|54.73|N|140|32|19.62|E|}}) * **Yenaki Iwa** – A stone said to have the power to silence a crying child. ({{Coord|40|18|54.42|N|140|32|10.97|E|}}) * **Usa Shrine** – A small shrine near the first torii where a small grass sickle is offered to cure smallpox in children. ({{Coord|40|18|53.77|N|140|32|04.32|E|}}) * **The First Torii** – A large stone torii; historically, a pond and garden existed to its right. ({{Coord|40|18|54.02|N|140|31|59.77|E|}}) * **Denjuin** – As recorded by Sugae Masumi, an illustration depicts Denjuin to the left of the first torii. This structure once existed between the first torii and the former pond and is said to mark the beginning of the mountain climbing route.<ref name="meisyo">“Matsumine Mountain Scenic Tour Association” (record, June 16, Heisei 3) by the Matsumine Town Association</ref> * **Cedar Alley** – A row of giant cedars between the first torii and the main shrine building. Although not mentioned in Sugae Masumi’s writings, old maps clearly depict it. Currently, the largest cedar is approximately 6.5 m in circumference and is over 600 years old. ({{Coord|40|18|53.18|N|140|31|56.64|E|}}) * **Stone Steps** – Approximately 170 stone steps (commonly stated as 160), also known as “Ishinokizahashi.”<ref name="matu"/> * **Fudō-no-Taki** – The waterfall of Fudō on the right side of the stone steps, whose water flows from a sheer cliff and eventually becomes Haragawa. Worshipers use it for purification before ascending to the main shrine. ({{Coord|40|18|52.91|N|140|31|53.66|E|}}) * **Uga Shrine** – A small stone shrine located to the right, along the waterfall’s flow, known as Uga no Kami; it is also called the small water shrine of Uga. ({{Coord|40|18|52.91|N|140|31|53.66|E|}}) * **Main Shrine Building** – The shrine grounds cover an area of 6 tan 11 bu, and the current main building was constructed by Satake Yoshinori starting in Meiji 3 and completed in April of Meiji 4. ({{Coord|40|18|52.23|N|140|31|50.23|E|}}) * **Yakushidō** – Located to the upper left of the main shrine building, also known as Hisu Shrine; dedicated to Yakushi Nyorai. ({{Coord|40|18|51.39|N|140|31|50.11|E|}}) * **Yama Shrine** – A small shrine dedicated to the mountain deity located to the right of the main building; proceeding around it leads to the source of Fudō-no-Taki. ({{Coord|40|18|52.87|N|140|31|50.84|E|}}) * **Iwaya Jūimen Kannon** – From the middle of the Cedar Alley, a side path leads to a large rock cave at the foot of the mountain, enshrining the Eleven-Faced Kannon. ({{Coord|40|18|50.03|N|140|31|57.18|E|}}) * **Shiroiwa** – A sheer white rock cliff to the left of the cave. * **Tenjin no Iwa** – A rock on the northern peak where ancient pines and other trees grow, known as Tenjin Rock. * **Higashi Nozoki Iwa (Eastern Lookout Rock)** – A massive rock jutting out to provide a view of the eastern sky. ({{Coord|40|18|59.12|N|140|31|46.83|E|}}) * **Kagami Iwa** – A rock that stands like a mirror; also referred to as Eboshi Iwa, due to its unusual shape. ({{Coord|40|18|59.18|N|140|31|46.67|E|}}) * **Tainai Kugu (Inner Womb Cave)** – A cave-like opening in the rock, said to evoke the feeling of being within a mother’s womb. ({{Coord|40|18|59.08|N|140|31|46.21|E|}}) * **Hokoku Iwa** – Located north of Tainai Kugu near the resting area; recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Nozoki Iwa” or “Byōbu Iwa,” where a “nozoki shugyō” similar to that of Ōmine-san was practiced. ({{Coord|40|18|59.58|N|140|31|43.35|E|}}) * **Kyūjō** – Near the summit, a slightly flat resting area where a triangular survey marker once stood. * **Kineiwa** – To the west of the resting area, a rock resembling a mortar carried by a moon rabbit. (Currently obscured by trees; on the western slope.) * **Okunoin** – Stairs on the western side of the resting area leading to an inner sanctuary called Okunoin (recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Oku no Goza”). From here, ancient features such as the Goma steps, a Zazen stone, and the rock of Gongen were once noted, though they are no longer identifiable. * **Suzuri Iwa** – Descending from the summit toward the south, a rock with a concave bottom that always contains water, known as Kōbō’s inkstone. (Near Ōiwa on a neighboring southeastern peak; now obscured by vegetation.) * **Kengami Mine** – A sharp rock outcrop with little foothold, described by Sugae Masumi as “Kengamine.” ({{Coord|40|18|42.71|N|140|31|49.76|E|}}) * **Tengu Iwa** – The large rocks on Kengami Mine are called Tengu Rock, with the larger one known as Great Tengu and the smaller as Little Tengu. (As recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Daitengu, Shōtengu no Iwa”.) * **Hasami Iwa** – Rocks facing each other resembling scissors; encountered along a small, relatively flat path obstructed by a large rock. ({{Coord|40|18|39.93|N|140|31|49.45|E|}}) * **Tengu-bashi** – Also known as the Tengu Suspension Bridge, it is the most scenic spot on the mountain. A massive rock bridges a deep chasm; crossing it offers a daunting view below. (Recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Daitengu no Tsuri-bashi.”) ({{Coord|40|18|37.95|N|140|31|51.35|E|}}) * **Tsuzumi Iwa** – A flat rock encountered when descending from Tengu Iwa, which produces a drum-like sound when stepped upon. (Recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Kago Iwa” and also as Tsuzumi Iwa.) ({{Coord|40|18|34.86|N|140|31|51.11|E|}}) After descending from Tsuzumi Iwa and turning left, one emerges below the First Torii and reaches the original road.<ref>『釈迦内郷土誌』, Shakani Kominkan, pp.265–269, composed during the Taishō era and reprinted in Heisei 1.</ref> == Sankokuga (Three-hooked Bell) == Sankokuga is an ancient bell excavated from Matsumine-san, which was presented to the Satake clan during the Edo period and is now housed in the {{ill|Tokyo National Museum|ja|東京国立博物館|12=draft}}. A receipt document from the Satake clan is recorded in the "Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi," and the "Hu Yin Onko-shi" confirms its existence. Locally, it is known as the "Station Bell" (Ekiro no Suzu). When [[Hitomi Shōu]] visited the region in 1797 (Kansei 9), he remarked that he had only heard of the Station Bell, and later Nikaidō Shokushima, in 1800 (Kansei 12), witnessed it and noted that it was housed at Seitōin in Kashima District or belonged to Matsumine-san in Dewa Akita-gun. He mentioned that it was unearthed in Tanaka about 100 years ago, and an elderly man from western regions confirmed that it was essentially identical to the bell from Kashima, hence the name "Station Bell" became established.<ref name="hinai"/> There is also a scholarly paper titled "On the Ancient Bell Housed by the Satake Family" discussing its true nature, though no definitive conclusion has been reached. This bell was transferred from the Satake family between April 24 and May 16, 1999 (Heisei 11) to the Tokyo National Museum, and was exhibited in the "Sankokuga Homecoming Exhibition" at the Ōdate Local Museum. According to some records in the "Kubota-gun Eki-ki," "Akita Fudoki," and "Gyōson Shiryaku," the bell was buried due to an earthquake, and an iron alligator was also excavated alongside it.<ref name="hinai"/> == Denjuin == Denjuin is recorded as the local temple of Matsumine-san. Sugae Masumi left an illustration of Denjuin, depicting it to the left of the First Torii when viewed from the base of the mountain. By the time the "Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi" was compiled, Denjuin had already been abolished. In {{ill|1598 AD|ja|1598th year|12=draft}}, when the Asari clan perished and Ōdate came under the control of Akita Miki, Denjuin received a total of 70 shaku from the Akita clan. This indicates that Matsumine-san had been widely venerated in the Hinai region since the Asari era or earlier, independent of the Asari clan. During the Edo period, documents record that the Satake clan of Ōdate provided 9 shaku and two retinues.<ref name="hinai"/> == Fudō-dō == Fudō-dō is the main shrine building of Matsumine-san. According to records in the "Kubota-gun Eki-ki," "Akita Fudoki," and "Gyōson Shiryaku," it burned down in {{ill|1786 AD|ja|1786th year|12=draft}} (Tenmei 6). According to a document titled "Shoshokurichū-chō," Fudō-dō also burned down on the night of April 8, 1863 (Bunkyū 3) due to a fire, resulting in the loss of the Fudō statue, and the local Denjuin was ordered by the Satake clan to observe 50 days of mourning. Fudō-dō was reconstructed in {{ill|1867 AD|ja|1867th year|12=draft}} (Keiō 3). Timber was felled from within Matsumine-san, and contributions were solicited from the surrounding area. However, in 1868 (Keiō 4, Meiji 1), during the Akita War when Ōdate City was burned and amid the anti-Buddhist ({{ill|Haibutsu Kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈|1=Haibutsu kishaku|12=draft}}) movement, although contributions of 180 ryo were collected at the time of reconstruction, by the time of the Fudō-dō relocation in 1871 only 1 ryo 2 bu was raised, indicating severe economic hardship.<ref name="hinai"/> Once a {{ill|Shingon sect|ja|真言宗|12=draft}} temple known as Matsumine-san, it was later converted to a shrine in accordance with the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, with the principal deity changed to {{ill|Tsukuyomi|ja|月夜見命|12=draft}}, and the name was changed to Matsumine Shrine. == Yakushi Shrine == Yakushi Shrine, also known as Hisu Shrine, is located on a small rise to the left of the main shrine building. It enshrines two statues of Yakushi Nyorai, which were donated in the Shōho Besshoku year (【1646 AD】) and in the Hōreki 10th year (【1760 AD】). In addition, many small stones with holes or inscribed with “me” are offered. A spring known as "Yakusui" is found midway up the steps; it is customary to purify one’s eyes with this water.<ref name="matu"/> == Tengu-sama == Among the many giant cedar and pine trees on Matsumine-san, one particularly distinctive giant cedar, known locally as the "Tengu Cedar," was reputed to have a hollow interior that served as the dwelling of tengu. However, as the tree died, it was cut down in Taishō 6, and the felled trunk was donated to Matsumine Shrine as a memorial. It is estimated to have had a diameter of nearly 3 m. During the Pacific War, families of soldiers—especially those whose relatives served in aviation units—visited the shrine and offered white and red paper fans in the hope of emulating the tengu’s ability to fly freely. It was also widely visited by families for protection against enemy bullets, due to the tengu’s reputed supernatural powers.<ref name="matu"/> == Suijin Shrine == Suijin Shrine is a small stone shrine located to the right, just before the stone steps. Known as Wakami, it is said that drinking water from here will restore youth; this tradition continues today on New Year’s Day.<ref name="matu"/> == Gosai == Gosai is a commemorative monument located to the left of the stone steps. There are no other monuments of its kind in Akita Prefecture. It is attributed to Emperor Uda. ({{Coord|40|18|51.82|N|140|31|51.31|E|}}) == Inari Shrine == The village shrine (satoyama) of Matsumine Shrine is an Inari Shrine, currently located in the western part of the Matsumine settlement ({{Coord|40|18|25.3|N|140|32|47.27|E|}}). Its enshrined deities are {{ill|Kura Inadama no Mikoto|ja|倉稲魂神|12=draft}}, {{ill|Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Ōmiya-uru no Mikoto|ja|大宮売命|12=draft}}. Its festival is held every October 10. Within its precincts there are monuments such as a stele of Sarutahiko, a “Twenty-Three Night Stele” (also known as Tsukimai-to), and a stone monument featuring a horse head.<ref name="matu"/> At the Inari Shrine, there are three dolls made of straw and pampas grass, with a history of approximately 450 years. Every last Sunday in November, the Matsumine settlement holds a doll festival. According to tradition, about 800 years ago, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitsune|ja|源義経|12=draft}}, accompanied by {{ill|Musashibō Benkei|ja|武蔵坊弁慶|12=draft}} and {{ill|Nasu no Yoichi|ja|那須与一|12=draft}}, passed through this area, inspiring the local people to create dolls out of reverence. These dolls were originally placed at the three entrances to the settlement to ward off epidemics and evil spirits, and were later enshrined within the Inari Shrine during the early Taishō period.<ref>「広報おおだて」, Shōwa 61, April 16</ref> == Records by Sugae Masumi and the Matumine-san Faith Sites == In June 1803 (Kyōwa 3), Sugae Masumi visited Matsumine-san and recorded his impressions in "Nie Nō Jikagarami." He noted, "On April 8, when a ceremony is held, many people come to worship at the main shrine. In the old days, those local Upase people who had not yet ascended to Nara’s Ōmine or Katsuragi would chant 'sange sange' and adorn themselves with prayer beads, bells, headscarves, and ayahikasa, carrying a dango-staff along with a spiral staff and a scepter, as they entered this peak." == Yamada Keizō == Marathon runner Yamada Keizō, from Ōdate City, who won the Boston Marathon in 1953 with a world record time, practiced running up and down the stone steps of Matsumine Shrine in his youth.<ref>Ōdate City, “Shakani Fieldwork – Matsumine Shrine Edition” [https://common3.pref.akita.lg.jp/genkimura/blog/?p=45876]</ref> == Matsumine Settlement and Matsumine Mine == The Matsumine Settlement, formerly known as Tanaka Village, was located at the confluence of the Shimonakagawa and Hanaokagawa rivers, about 300 m from the village. In 1963, a black ore deposit extending approximately 3000 mt was discovered 250–300 m underground beneath the settlement. Due to mining, subsidence occurred, and by 1976, 85 households were collectively relocated to the present site. In 1973, Matsumine Station was opened in the vicinity. Matsumine Mine extracted black ore from the Ōyama ore deposit using an open-column (open-pit) method. In 1932, its annual output surpassed that of the Ashio Copper Mine, and in 1970 it achieved a national record of 16,285 t per year. In 1979, despite aging facilities and maintenance expenses, soaring metal prices led to high revenues of 2.28 billion yen. However, due to a downturn in metal prices, the mine was closed in 1994 (Heisei 6), while leaving some reserves intact. During the Taishō period, this area suffered from severe smog caused by emissions from Kosaka Mine and Hanaoka Mine; the Matsumine area was the worst affected. Matsumine-san suffered greatly, with all its pine and chestnut trees dying, and in 1915 (Taishō 4) the entire mountain was deforested, leading to extensive reforestation. The history of this event is detailed on a commemorative monument by the shrine's stone steps.<ref name="matu"/> == Ōyama == {{Infobox Mountain |Name = Ōyama |image = [[File:Ôyama(Ôdate si).jpg|250px]] |image Caption = Ōyama in Ōdate City (Matsumine-san) |Elevation = 375.6 m |Coordinates = {{coord|40|18|52.9|N|140|31|43.2|E|type:mountain_region:JP|display=inline}} |Location = {{JPN}}<br />{{ill|Akita Prefecture|ja|秋田県|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ōdate City|ja|大館市|12=draft}}, Matsumine Ōyama |Mountain Range = |Type = |First Ascent = |Map = {{Location map|Japan Akita Prefecture#Japan|relief=1|float=center}}{{日本の位置情報|40|18|53.05|140|31|43.2|Ōyama|40.314737,140.528669|Ōyama|nocoord=yes}} }} The highest peak of Matsumine-san is Ōyama (375.7 m), which epitomizes the very notion of a "mountain." On Ōyama, there is a pine known as the "Makka Pine," which, upon reaching 62 years of age, is said to be designated as such. Additionally, unusually for a mountain of roughly 300 m class, about 100 native {{ill|Buna|ja|ブナ|12=draft}} trees grow here<ref name="matu"/>. Although the number of trees is small, Ōyama is home to many rare and endangered plant species, including {{ill|Urashima-sō|ja|ウラシマソウ|12=draft}}, {{ill|Shōjōbakama|ja|ショウジョウバカマ|12=draft}}, {{ill|Kuramayuri|ja|クルマユリ|12=draft}}, {{ill|Iwanashi|ja|イワナシ|12=draft}}, {{ill|Yamazaki-sō|ja|ヤマザキソウ|12=draft}}, {{ill|Shunran|ja|シュンラン|12=draft}}, {{ill|Kakiran|ja|カキラン|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ginran|ja|ギンラン|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ruiyōbotan|ja|ルイヨウボタン|12=draft}}, {{ill|Jakōsō|ja|ジャコウソウ|12=draft}}, {{ill|Kumokiriso|ja|クモキリソウ|12=draft}}, {{ill|Jigabachisō|ja|ジガバチソウ|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ginryōsō|ja|ギンリョウソウ|12=draft}}, {{ill|Iwauchiwa|ja|イワウチワ|12=draft}}, {{ill|Sasabaginran|ja|ササバギンラン|12=draft}}, {{ill|Azumagiku|ja|アヅマギク|12=draft}}, {{ill|Akabanamaru Bamanasaku|ja|アカバナマルバマンサク|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Kumagaisho|ja|クマガイソウ|12=draft}}, among others.<ref name="matu"/> At the summit of Ōyama stands the Ōdate Television Relay Station / Hanaya FM Relay. == Matsumine-san Faith Sites Image Gallery == <gallery> File:Matuminesan Kagamiiwa.jpg | Kagami Iwa File:Ôyama Santyô.jpg | The summit of Ōyama with television towers in the background File:Matumine Zinzya Iti no Torii.jpg | The first torii (an illustration by Sugae Masumi from a similar location) File:Matumine Iwaya Zyûitimen Kannon.jpg | Shrine for the Jūimen Kannon at Iwaya (the Kannon statue is no longer present) File:Matumine Inari Zinzya.jpg | Matsumine Shrine's village Inari Shrine </gallery> == Footnotes ==

'''Matumine Shrine''' ({{ill|Matumine Shrine|ja|松峰神社|12=draft|12=draft}}) is a Shinto shrine located in Matsumine, Oyamagai, Ōdate City, {{ill|Akita Prefecture|ja|秋田県|12=draft|12=draft}}.
'''Matumine-san Faith Sites''' ({{ill|Matumine-san Shinkō Iseki-gun|ja|松峰山信仰遺跡群|12=draft|12=draft}}) refers to the group of ancient and medieval esoteric ({{ill|Mikkyo|ja|密教|12=draft|12=draft}}) sites associated with auspicious legends that cluster around Matumine Shrine. The mountain, named after the honzon of the shrine—{{ill|Fudō Myōō|ja|不動明王|1=Acala|lt=Fudō Myōō|2=ja|3=不動明王|12=draft|12=draft}} of the former Ryouakkosan Dainenji—has its central peak, Ōyama, at an elevation of 375.7 m. The village shrine (satoyama) located at 141-5, Nioida, Ōdate City, is now known as the Matsumine {{ill|Inari Shrine|ja|稲荷神社|12=draft|12=draft}}. Matumine-san Faith Sites were designated as a historic site by Ōdate City on May 1, 2009 (Heisei 21), with coordinates based on the designated cultural property map. During the Edo period, it was known as "Matsumine Kureyuki" in the Eight Views of Ōdate and served as the 32nd sacred site in the Akita Rokugun Sanjū Sankannon Reijō.
== Legend == The honzon of Matumine Shrine is Fudō Myōō (attributed to the works of {{ill|Kōbō Daishi|ja|弘法大師|12=draft|12=draft}}) accompanied by two guardian child deities.
== Enshrined Deities and Subsidiary Shrines == * Honzon: Fudō Myōō (伝弘法大師作) and two guardian child deities (Zenritsu Nīdōji) * Subsidiary shrines include: Yakushidō, the mountain deity shrine, Uga Shrine, Kurikara Fudō Taki (whose waterfall becomes Haragawa), Iwaya Jūimen Kannon (attributed to Kōbō Daishi), and Shō Kannon (attributed to Senchō).
== History == In {{ill|817 AD|ja|817th year|12=draft|12=draft}} (Kōnin 8), {{ill|Kōbō Daishi|ja|弘法大師|12=draft|12=draft}} is said to have founded the mountain. He cast a bronze statue of Amida Kannon and made a mirror out of silver, naming it Daienkō. In {{ill|822 AD|ja|822nd year|12=draft|12=draft}} (Kōnin 13), the Left Minister Seikō-shaden was constructed. In March {{ill|857 AD|ja|857th year|12=draft|12=draft}} (Tennan 1), an earthquake buried all existing structures. In {{ill|891 AD|ja|891st year|12=draft|12=draft}} (Kanpei 3), Emperor Uda granted a headband to Ono Yoshimitsu, the son of Ono Yoshiya (father of Ono Komachi). That same year, a manuscript inscribed with “Yamashi no Hikari mo Toki ni Umamaruru, Araware Terase Matsumine no Tsuki” was presented. In {{ill|895 AD|ja|895th year|12=draft|12=draft}} (Kanpei 7), Ono Yoshifusa was appointed as the official, and the shrine building was constructed.
Afterwards, the subsequent history remains obscure for several centuries. In {{ill|1403 AD|ja|1403rd year|12=draft|12=draft}} (Ōei 10), the local lord of the {{ill|Asari clan|ja|浅利氏|12=draft|12=draft}} began to revere the shrine, and in the first year of Kei'an the Satake clan, devotees of Fudō, transformed the main shrine into a Buddhist temple hall. During the Kansei era, a monk from Denshūin discovered a bell in the soil. In {{ill|1801 AD|ja|1801st year|12=draft|12=draft}} (Kyōwa 1), the feudal lord Satake Yoshikazu presented this bell during a tour of his domain. In the 3rd year of the Meiji era, the Buddhist Fudō was abolished. For the regular festivals, items from the former domain were provided. In {{ill|1873 AD|ja|1873rd year|12=draft|12=draft}} (Meiji 6), the shrine was reclassified as a village shrine. The current enshrined deity is {{ill|Tsukuyomi|ja|月読大神|12=draft|12=draft}}. The main shrine building was formerly known as Furuta Nakamura, but it later adopted the name Matsumine Shrine, after the mountain on which it stands.<ref>『釈迦内郷土誌』, Shakani Kominkan, pp.93–95</ref>
The komainu at the main shrine were donated by {{ill|Itahabutakesuke|ja|伊多波武助|12=draft|12=draft}}.<ref>『秋田ふしぎ探訪』, Mumyōsha Publishing, 1979</ref>
== “Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi” == Numerous ancient texts record the legends of Matsumine-san. Representative texts include: * ''Akita Rokugun Sanjū Sankannon Junrei-ki''<ref>Kyōhō era (1716–1736), [{{NDLDC|1174121/16}}] in Akita Sōsho Vol.8 and in Shin Akita Sōsho Vol.3</ref> * ''Kubota-gun Eki-ki'' * ''Akita Fudoki'' * ''Gyōson Shiryaku'' * “Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi”<ref name="hinai">『大館郷土博物館研究紀要 火内』 Vol.12, March 2015, pp.13–29, “Materials on Matsumine-san Faith,” from the Matsumine-san Shinkō Iseki-gun Examination Subcommittee of the Ōdate City Cultural Property Protection Council</ref>
Other notable features on Matsumine-san include: * **Haragawa** – A small stream flowing from the waterfall of Fudō located on the right side below the stone steps of the approach. The waterfall is so named because it is used to wash away impurities from worshipers. ({{Coord|40|18|43.02|N|140|32|48.01|E|}}) * **Shinmeisha** – A small shrine on a hill about one chō (approximately 100 m) from the foot of the mountain; also called O-Ise-sama. ({{Coord|40|18|50.71|N|140|32|31.59|E|}}) * **Yuden-yama** – A distant monument to Yuden-yama, established in {{ill|1770 AD|ja|1770th year|12=draft|12=draft}}. ({{Coord|40|18|48.76|N|140|32|35.53|E|}}) * **Kōshin-zuka** – A mound established in {{ill|1778 AD|ja|1778th year|12=draft|12=draft}}. ({{Coord|40|18|48.61|N|140|32|34.72|E|}}) * **Okoishi and Obaishi** – Stones enshrining {{ill|Manjushri|ja|文殊菩薩|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Fugen Bosatsu|ja|普賢菩薩|12=draft|12=draft}}. ({{Coord|40|18|54.11|N|140|32|20.70|E|}}) and ({{Coord|40|18|54.73|N|140|32|19.62|E|}}) * **Yenaki Iwa** – A stone said to have the power to silence a crying child. ({{Coord|40|18|54.42|N|140|32|10.97|E|}}) * **Usa Shrine** – A small shrine near the first torii where a small grass sickle is offered to cure smallpox in children. ({{Coord|40|18|53.77|N|140|32|04.32|E|}}) * **The First Torii** – A large stone torii; historically, a pond and garden existed to its right. ({{Coord|40|18|54.02|N|140|31|59.77|E|}}) * **Denjuin** – As recorded by Sugae Masumi, an illustration depicts Denjuin to the left of the first torii. This structure once existed between the first torii and the former pond and is said to mark the beginning of the mountain climbing route.<ref name="meisyo">“Matsumine Mountain Scenic Tour Association” (record, June 16, Heisei 3) by the Matsumine Town Association</ref> * **Cedar Alley** – A row of giant cedars between the first torii and the main shrine building. Although not mentioned in Sugae Masumi’s writings, old maps clearly depict it. Currently, the largest cedar is approximately 6.5 m in circumference and is over 600 years old. ({{Coord|40|18|53.18|N|140|31|56.64|E|}}) * **Stone Steps** – Approximately 170 stone steps (commonly stated as 160), also known as “Ishinokizahashi.”<ref name="matu"/> * **Fudō-no-Taki** – The waterfall of Fudō on the right side of the stone steps, whose water flows from a sheer cliff and eventually becomes Haragawa. Worshipers use it for purification before ascending to the main shrine. ({{Coord|40|18|52.91|N|140|31|53.66|E|}}) * **Uga Shrine** – A small stone shrine located to the right, along the waterfall’s flow, known as Uga no Kami; it is also called the small water shrine of Uga. ({{Coord|40|18|52.91|N|140|31|53.66|E|}}) * **Main Shrine Building** – The shrine grounds cover an area of 6 tan 11 bu, and the current main building was constructed by Satake Yoshinori starting in Meiji 3 and completed in April of Meiji 4. ({{Coord|40|18|52.23|N|140|31|50.23|E|}}) * **Yakushidō** – Located to the upper left of the main shrine building, also known as Hisu Shrine; dedicated to Yakushi Nyorai. ({{Coord|40|18|51.39|N|140|31|50.11|E|}}) * **Yama Shrine** – A small shrine dedicated to the mountain deity located to the right of the main building; proceeding around it leads to the source of Fudō-no-Taki. ({{Coord|40|18|52.87|N|140|31|50.84|E|}}) * **Iwaya Jūimen Kannon** – From the middle of the Cedar Alley, a side path leads to a large rock cave at the foot of the mountain, enshrining the Eleven-Faced Kannon. ({{Coord|40|18|50.03|N|140|31|57.18|E|}}) * **Shiroiwa** – A sheer white rock cliff to the left of the cave. * **Tenjin no Iwa** – A rock on the northern peak where ancient pines and other trees grow, known as Tenjin Rock. * **Higashi Nozoki Iwa (Eastern Lookout Rock)** – A massive rock jutting out to provide a view of the eastern sky. ({{Coord|40|18|59.12|N|140|31|46.83|E|}}) * **Kagami Iwa** – A rock that stands like a mirror; also referred to as Eboshi Iwa, due to its unusual shape. ({{Coord|40|18|59.18|N|140|31|46.67|E|}}) * **Tainai Kugu (Inner Womb Cave)** – A cave-like opening in the rock, said to evoke the feeling of being within a mother’s womb. ({{Coord|40|18|59.08|N|140|31|46.21|E|}}) * **Hokoku Iwa** – Located north of Tainai Kugu near the resting area; recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Nozoki Iwa” or “Byōbu Iwa,” where a “nozoki shugyō” similar to that of Ōmine-san was practiced. ({{Coord|40|18|59.58|N|140|31|43.35|E|}}) * **Kyūjō** – Near the summit, a slightly flat resting area where a triangular survey marker once stood. * **Kineiwa** – To the west of the resting area, a rock resembling a mortar carried by a moon rabbit. (Currently obscured by trees; on the western slope.) * **Okunoin** – Stairs on the western side of the resting area leading to an inner sanctuary called Okunoin (recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Oku no Goza”). From here, ancient features such as the Goma steps, a Zazen stone, and the rock of Gongen were once noted, though they are no longer identifiable. * **Suzuri Iwa** – Descending from the summit toward the south, a rock with a concave bottom that always contains water, known as Kōbō’s inkstone. (Near Ōiwa on a neighboring southeastern peak; now obscured by vegetation.) * **Kengami Mine** – A sharp rock outcrop with little foothold, described by Sugae Masumi as “Kengamine.” ({{Coord|40|18|42.71|N|140|31|49.76|E|}}) * **Tengu Iwa** – The large rocks on Kengami Mine are called Tengu Rock, with the larger one known as Great Tengu and the smaller as Little Tengu. (As recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Daitengu, Shōtengu no Iwa”.) * **Hasami Iwa** – Rocks facing each other resembling scissors; encountered along a small, relatively flat path obstructed by a large rock. ({{Coord|40|18|39.93|N|140|31|49.45|E|}}) * **Tengu-bashi** – Also known as the Tengu Suspension Bridge, it is the most scenic spot on the mountain. A massive rock bridges a deep chasm; crossing it offers a daunting view below. (Recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Daitengu no Tsuri-bashi.”) ({{Coord|40|18|37.95|N|140|31|51.35|E|}}) * **Tsuzumi Iwa** – A flat rock encountered when descending from Tengu Iwa, which produces a drum-like sound when stepped upon. (Recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Kago Iwa” and also as Tsuzumi Iwa.) ({{Coord|40|18|34.86|N|140|31|51.11|E|}}) After descending from Tsuzumi Iwa and turning left, one emerges below the First Torii and reaches the original road.<ref>『釈迦内郷土誌』, Shakani Kominkan, pp.265–269, composed during the Taishō era and reprinted in Heisei 1.</ref> == Sankokuga (Three-hooked Bell) == Sankokuga is an ancient bell excavated from Matsumine-san, which was presented to the Satake clan during the Edo period and is now housed in the {{ill|Tokyo National Museum|ja|東京国立博物館|12=draft|12=draft}}. A receipt document from the Satake clan is recorded in the "Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi," and the "Hu Yin Onko-shi" confirms its existence. Locally, it is known as the "Station Bell" (Ekiro no Suzu). When [[Hitomi Shōu]] visited the region in 1797 (Kansei 9), he remarked that he had only heard of the Station Bell, and later Nikaidō Shokushima, in 1800 (Kansei 12), witnessed it and noted that it was housed at Seitōin in Kashima District or belonged to Matsumine-san in Dewa Akita-gun. He mentioned that it was unearthed in Tanaka about 100 years ago, and an elderly man from western regions confirmed that it was essentially identical to the bell from Kashima, hence the name "Station Bell" became established.<ref name="hinai"/> There is also a scholarly paper titled "On the Ancient Bell Housed by the Satake Family" discussing its true nature, though no definitive conclusion has been reached. This bell was transferred from the Satake family between April 24 and May 16, 1999 (Heisei 11) to the Tokyo National Museum, and was exhibited in the "Sankokuga Homecoming Exhibition" at the Ōdate Local Museum. According to some records in the "Kubota-gun Eki-ki," "Akita Fudoki," and "Gyōson Shiryaku," the bell was buried due to an earthquake, and an iron alligator was also excavated alongside it.<ref name="hinai"/> == Denjuin == Denjuin is recorded as the local temple of Matsumine-san. Sugae Masumi left an illustration of Denjuin, depicting it to the left of the First Torii when viewed from the base of the mountain. By the time the "Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi" was compiled, Denjuin had already been abolished. In {{ill|1598 AD|ja|1598th year|12=draft|12=draft}}, when the Asari clan perished and Ōdate came under the control of Akita Miki, Denjuin received a total of 70 shaku from the Akita clan. This indicates that Matsumine-san had been widely venerated in the Hinai region since the Asari era or earlier, independent of the Asari clan. During the Edo period, documents record that the Satake clan of Ōdate provided 9 shaku and two retinues.<ref name="hinai"/> == Fudō-dō == Fudō-dō is the main shrine building of Matsumine-san. According to records in the "Kubota-gun Eki-ki," "Akita Fudoki," and "Gyōson Shiryaku," it burned down in {{ill|1786 AD|ja|1786th year|12=draft|12=draft}} (Tenmei 6). According to a document titled "Shoshokurichū-chō," Fudō-dō also burned down on the night of April 8, 1863 (Bunkyū 3) due to a fire, resulting in the loss of the Fudō statue, and the local Denjuin was ordered by the Satake clan to observe 50 days of mourning. Fudō-dō was reconstructed in {{ill|1867 AD|ja|1867th year|12=draft|12=draft}} (Keiō 3). Timber was felled from within Matsumine-san, and contributions were solicited from the surrounding area. However, in 1868 (Keiō 4, Meiji 1), during the Akita War when Ōdate City was burned and amid the anti-Buddhist ({{ill|Haibutsu Kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈|1=Haibutsu kishaku|12=draft|12=draft}}) movement, although contributions of 180 ryo were collected at the time of reconstruction, by the time of the Fudō-dō relocation in 1871 only 1 ryo 2 bu was raised, indicating severe economic hardship.<ref name="hinai"/> Once a {{ill|Shingon sect|ja|真言宗|12=draft|12=draft}} temple known as Matsumine-san, it was later converted to a shrine in accordance with the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, with the principal deity changed to {{ill|Tsukuyomi|ja|月夜見命|12=draft|12=draft}}, and the name was changed to Matsumine Shrine. == Yakushi Shrine == Yakushi Shrine, also known as Hisu Shrine, is located on a small rise to the left of the main shrine building. It enshrines two statues of Yakushi Nyorai, which were donated in the Shōho Besshoku year (【1646 AD】) and in the Hōreki 10th year (【1760 AD】). In addition, many small stones with holes or inscribed with “me” are offered. A spring known as "Yakusui" is found midway up the steps; it is customary to purify one’s eyes with this water.<ref name="matu"/> == Tengu-sama == Among the many giant cedar and pine trees on Matsumine-san, one particularly distinctive giant cedar, known locally as the "Tengu Cedar," was reputed to have a hollow interior that served as the dwelling of tengu. However, as the tree died, it was cut down in Taishō 6, and the felled trunk was donated to Matsumine Shrine as a memorial. It is estimated to have had a diameter of nearly 3 m. During the Pacific War, families of soldiers—especially those whose relatives served in aviation units—visited the shrine and offered white and red paper fans in the hope of emulating the tengu’s ability to fly freely. It was also widely visited by families for protection against enemy bullets, due to the tengu’s reputed supernatural powers.<ref name="matu"/> == Suijin Shrine == Suijin Shrine is a small stone shrine located to the right, just before the stone steps. Known as Wakami, it is said that drinking water from here will restore youth; this tradition continues today on New Year’s Day.<ref name="matu"/> == Gosai == Gosai is a commemorative monument located to the left of the stone steps. There are no other monuments of its kind in Akita Prefecture. It is attributed to Emperor Uda. ({{Coord|40|18|51.82|N|140|31|51.31|E|}}) == Inari Shrine == The village shrine (satoyama) of Matsumine Shrine is an Inari Shrine, currently located in the western part of the Matsumine settlement ({{Coord|40|18|25.3|N|140|32|47.27|E|}}). Its enshrined deities are {{ill|Kura Inadama no Mikoto|ja|倉稲魂神|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦|12=draft|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Ōmiya-uru no Mikoto|ja|大宮売命|12=draft|12=draft}}. Its festival is held every October 10. Within its precincts there are monuments such as a stele of Sarutahiko, a “Twenty-Three Night Stele” (also known as Tsukimai-to), and a stone monument featuring a horse head.<ref name="matu"/> At the Inari Shrine, there are three dolls made of straw and pampas grass, with a history of approximately 450 years. Every last Sunday in November, the Matsumine settlement holds a doll festival. According to tradition, about 800 years ago, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitsune|ja|源義経|12=draft|12=draft}}, accompanied by {{ill|Musashibō Benkei|ja|武蔵坊弁慶|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Nasu no Yoichi|ja|那須与一|12=draft|12=draft}}, passed through this area, inspiring the local people to create dolls out of reverence. These dolls were originally placed at the three entrances to the settlement to ward off epidemics and evil spirits, and were later enshrined within the Inari Shrine during the early Taishō period.<ref>「広報おおだて」, Shōwa 61, April 16</ref> == Records by Sugae Masumi and the Matumine-san Faith Sites == In June 1803 (Kyōwa 3), Sugae Masumi visited Matsumine-san and recorded his impressions in "Nie Nō Jikagarami." He noted, "On April 8, when a ceremony is held, many people come to worship at the main shrine. In the old days, those local Upase people who had not yet ascended to Nara’s Ōmine or Katsuragi would chant 'sange sange' and adorn themselves with prayer beads, bells, headscarves, and ayahikasa, carrying a dango-staff along with a spiral staff and a scepter, as they entered this peak." == Yamada Keizō == Marathon runner Yamada Keizō, from Ōdate City, who won the Boston Marathon in 1953 with a world record time, practiced running up and down the stone steps of Matsumine Shrine in his youth.<ref>Ōdate City, “Shakani Fieldwork – Matsumine Shrine Edition” [https://common3.pref.akita.lg.jp/genkimura/blog/?p=45876]</ref> == Matsumine Settlement and Matsumine Mine == The Matsumine Settlement, formerly known as Tanaka Village, was located at the confluence of the Shimonakagawa and Hanaokagawa rivers, about 300 m from the village. In 1963, a black ore deposit extending approximately 3000 mt was discovered 250–300 m underground beneath the settlement. Due to mining, subsidence occurred, and by 1976, 85 households were collectively relocated to the present site. In 1973, Matsumine Station was opened in the vicinity. Matsumine Mine extracted black ore from the Ōyama ore deposit using an open-column (open-pit) method. In 1932, its annual output surpassed that of the Ashio Copper Mine, and in 1970 it achieved a national record of 16,285 t per year. In 1979, despite aging facilities and maintenance expenses, soaring metal prices led to high revenues of 2.28 billion yen. However, due to a downturn in metal prices, the mine was closed in 1994 (Heisei 6), while leaving some reserves intact. During the Taishō period, this area suffered from severe smog caused by emissions from Kosaka Mine and Hanaoka Mine; the Matsumine area was the worst affected. Matsumine-san suffered greatly, with all its pine and chestnut trees dying, and in 1915 (Taishō 4) the entire mountain was deforested, leading to extensive reforestation. The history of this event is detailed on a commemorative monument by the shrine's stone steps.<ref name="matu"/> == Ōyama == {{Infobox Mountain |Name = Ōyama |image = [[File:Ôyama(Ôdate si).jpg|250px]] |image Caption = Ōyama in Ōdate City (Matsumine-san) |Elevation = 375.6 m |Coordinates = {{coord|40|18|52.9|N|140|31|43.2|E|type:mountain_region:JP|display=inline}} |Location = {{JPN}}<br />{{ill|Akita Prefecture|ja|秋田県|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ōdate City|ja|大館市|12=draft|12=draft}}, Matsumine Ōyama |Mountain Range = |Type = |First Ascent = |Map = {{Location map|Japan Akita Prefecture#Japan|relief=1|float=center}}{{日本の位置情報|40|18|53.05|140|31|43.2|Ōyama|40.314737,140.528669|Ōyama|nocoord=yes}} }} The highest peak of Matsumine-san is Ōyama (375.7 m), which epitomizes the very notion of a "mountain." On Ōyama, there is a pine known as the "Makka Pine," which, upon reaching 62 years of age, is said to be designated as such. Additionally, unusually for a mountain of roughly 300 m class, about 100 native {{ill|Buna|ja|ブナ|12=draft|12=draft}} trees grow here<ref name="matu"/>. Although the number of trees is small, Ōyama is home to many rare and endangered plant species, including {{ill|Urashima-sō|ja|ウラシマソウ|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Shōjōbakama|ja|ショウジョウバカマ|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Kuramayuri|ja|クルマユリ|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Iwanashi|ja|イワナシ|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Yamazaki-sō|ja|ヤマザキソウ|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Shunran|ja|シュンラン|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Kakiran|ja|カキラン|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ginran|ja|ギンラン|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ruiyōbotan|ja|ルイヨウボタン|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Jakōsō|ja|ジャコウソウ|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Kumokiriso|ja|クモキリソウ|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Jigabachisō|ja|ジガバチソウ|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ginryōsō|ja|ギンリョウソウ|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Iwauchiwa|ja|イワウチワ|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Sasabaginran|ja|ササバギンラン|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Azumagiku|ja|アヅマギク|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Akabanamaru Bamanasaku|ja|アカバナマルバマンサク|12=draft|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Kumagaisho|ja|クマガイソウ|12=draft|12=draft}}, among others.<ref name="matu"/> At the summit of Ōyama stands the Ōdate Television Relay Station / Hanaya FM Relay. == Matsumine-san Faith Sites Image Gallery == <gallery> File:Matuminesan Kagamiiwa.jpg | Kagami Iwa File:Ôyama Santyô.jpg | The summit of Ōyama with television towers in the background File:Matumine Zinzya Iti no Torii.jpg | The first torii (an illustration by Sugae Masumi from a similar location) File:Matumine Iwaya Zyûitimen Kannon.jpg | Shrine for the Jūimen Kannon at Iwaya (the Kannon statue is no longer present) File:Matumine Inari Zinzya.jpg | Matsumine Shrine's village Inari Shrine </gallery> == Footnotes ==
