'''Matumine Shrine''' ({{ill|Matumine Shrine|ja|松峰神社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matumine Shrine|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) is a Shinto shrine located in Matsumine, Oyamagai, Ōdate City, [[:en:Akita Prefecture|Akita Prefecture]].
'''Matumine-san Faith Sites''' ({{ill|Matumine-san Shinkō Iseki-gun|ja|松峰山信仰遺跡群|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matumine-san Shinkō Iseki-gun|qq=|1=Ō Yama|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q67587030}}) refers to the group of ancient and medieval esoteric ([[:en:Mikkyō|Mikkyo]]) sites associated with auspicious legends that cluster around Matumine Shrine. The mountain, named after the honzon of the shrine—[[:en:Acala|Fudō Myōō]] of the former Ryouakkosan Dainenji—has its central peak, Ōyama, at an elevation of 375.7 m. The village shrine (satoyama) located at 141-5, Nioida, Ōdate City, is now known as the Matsumine [[:en:Inari shrine|Inari Shrine]]. Matumine-san Faith Sites were designated as a historic site by Ōdate City on May 1, 2009 (Heisei 21), with coordinates based on the designated cultural property map. During the Edo period, it was known as "Matsumine Kureyuki" in the Eight Views of Ōdate and served as the 32nd sacred site in the Akita Rokugun Sanjū Sankannon Reijō.
== Legend == The honzon of Matumine Shrine is Fudō Myōō (attributed to the works of {{ill|Kōbō Daishi|ja|弘法大師|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōbō Daishi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海|1=Kūkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q222227}}) accompanied by two guardian child deities.
== Enshrined Deities and Subsidiary Shrines == * Honzon: Fudō Myōō (伝弘法大師作) and two guardian child deities (Zenritsu Nīdōji) * Subsidiary shrines include: Yakushidō, the mountain deity shrine, Uga Shrine, Kurikara Fudō Taki (whose waterfall becomes Haragawa), Iwaya Jūimen Kannon (attributed to Kōbō Daishi), and Shō Kannon (attributed to Senchō).
== History == In [[:en:817|817 AD]] (Kōnin 8), {{ill|Kōbō Daishi|ja|弘法大師|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōbō Daishi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海|1=Kūkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q222227}} is said to have founded the mountain. He cast a bronze statue of Amida Kannon and made a mirror out of silver, naming it Daienkō. In [[:en:822|822 AD]] (Kōnin 13), the Left Minister Seikō-shaden was constructed. In March [[:en:857|857 AD]] (Tennan 1), an earthquake buried all existing structures. In [[:en:891|891 AD]] (Kanpei 3), Emperor Uda granted a headband to Ono Yoshimitsu, the son of Ono Yoshiya (father of Ono Komachi). That same year, a manuscript inscribed with “Yamashi no Hikari mo Toki ni Umamaruru, Araware Terase Matsumine no Tsuki” was presented. In [[:en:895|895 AD]] (Kanpei 7), Ono Yoshifusa was appointed as the official, and the shrine building was constructed.
Afterwards, the subsequent history remains obscure for several centuries. In [[:en:1403|1403 AD]] (Ōei 10), the local lord of the {{ill|Asari clan|ja|浅利氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Asari clan|qq=|1=Asari clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11557021}} began to revere the shrine, and in the first year of Kei'an the Satake clan, devotees of Fudō, transformed the main shrine into a Buddhist temple hall. During the Kansei era, a monk from Denshūin discovered a bell in the soil. In [[:en:1801|1801 AD]] (Kyōwa 1), the feudal lord Satake Yoshikazu presented this bell during a tour of his domain. In the 3rd year of the Meiji era, the Buddhist Fudō was abolished. For the regular festivals, items from the former domain were provided. In [[:en:1873|1873 AD]] (Meiji 6), the shrine was reclassified as a village shrine. The current enshrined deity is {{ill|Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|lt=Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|lt=Tsukuyomi|ja|月読大神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuyomi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. The main shrine building was formerly known as Furuta Nakamura, but it later adopted the name Matsumine Shrine, after the mountain on which it stands.<ref>『釈迦内郷土誌』, Shakani Kominkan, pp.93–95</ref>
The komainu at the main shrine were donated by {{ill|Itahabutakesuke|ja|伊多波武助|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Itahabutakesuke|qq=|1=Itaba Busuke|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24861288}}.<ref>『秋田ふしぎ探訪』, Mumyōsha Publishing, 1979</ref>
== “Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi” == Numerous ancient texts record the legends of Matsumine-san. Representative texts include: * ''Akita Rokugun Sanjū Sankannon Junrei-ki''<ref>Kyōhō era (1716–1736), [{{NDLDC|1174121/16}}] in Akita Sōsho Vol.8 and in Shin Akita Sōsho Vol.3</ref> * ''Kubota-gun Eki-ki'' * ''Akita Fudoki'' * ''Gyōson Shiryaku'' * “Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi”<ref name="hinai">『大館郷土博物館研究紀要 火内』 Vol.12, March 2015, pp.13–29, “Materials on Matsumine-san Faith,” from the Matsumine-san Shinkō Iseki-gun Examination Subcommittee of the Ōdate City Cultural Property Protection Council</ref>
Other notable features on Matsumine-san include: * '''Haragawa''' – A small stream flowing from the waterfall of Fudō located on the right side below the stone steps of the approach. The waterfall is so named because it is used to wash away impurities from worshipers. ({{Coord|40|18|43.02|N|140|32|48.01|E|}}) * '''Shinmeisha''' – A small shrine on a hill about one chō (approximately 100 m) from the foot of the mountain; also called O-Ise-sama. ({{Coord|40|18|50.71|N|140|32|31.59|E|}}) * '''Yuden-yama''' – A distant monument to Yuden-yama, established in [[:en:1770|1770 AD]]. ({{Coord|40|18|48.76|N|140|32|35.53|E|}}) * '''Kōshin-zuka''' – A mound established in [[:en:1778|1778 AD]]. ({{Coord|40|18|48.61|N|140|32|34.72|E|}}) * '''Okoishi and Obaishi''' – Stones enshrining [[:en:Manjushri|Manjushri]] and [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Fugen Bosatsu]]. ({{Coord|40|18|54.11|N|140|32|20.70|E|}}) and ({{Coord|40|18|54.73|N|140|32|19.62|E|}}) * '''Yenaki Iwa''' – A stone said to have the power to silence a crying child. ({{Coord|40|18|54.42|N|140|32|10.97|E|}}) * '''Usa Shrine''' – A small shrine near the first torii where a small grass sickle is offered to cure smallpox in children. ({{Coord|40|18|53.77|N|140|32|04.32|E|}}) * '''The First Torii''' – A large stone torii; historically, a pond and garden existed to its right. ({{Coord|40|18|54.02|N|140|31|59.77|E|}}) * '''Denjuin''' – As recorded by Sugae Masumi, an illustration depicts Denjuin to the left of the first torii. This structure once existed between the first torii and the former pond and is said to mark the beginning of the mountain climbing route.<ref name="meisyo">“Matsumine Mountain Scenic Tour Association” (record, June 16, Heisei 3) by the Matsumine Town Association</ref> * '''Cedar Alley''' – A row of giant cedars between the first torii and the main shrine building. Although not mentioned in Sugae Masumi’s writings, old maps clearly depict it. Currently, the largest cedar is approximately 6.5 m in circumference and is over 600 years old. ({{Coord|40|18|53.18|N|140|31|56.64|E|}}) * '''Stone Steps''' – Approximately 170 stone steps (commonly stated as 160), also known as “Ishinokizahashi.”<ref name="matu"/> * '''Fudō-no-Taki''' – The waterfall of Fudō on the right side of the stone steps, whose water flows from a sheer cliff and eventually becomes Haragawa. Worshipers use it for purification before ascending to the main shrine. ({{Coord|40|18|52.91|N|140|31|53.66|E|}}) * '''Uga Shrine''' – A small stone shrine located to the right, along the waterfall’s flow, known as Uga no Kami; it is also called the small water shrine of Uga. ({{Coord|40|18|52.91|N|140|31|53.66|E|}}) * '''Main Shrine Building''' – The shrine grounds cover an area of 6 tan 11 bu, and the current main building was constructed by Satake Yoshinori starting in Meiji 3 and completed in April of Meiji 4. ({{Coord|40|18|52.23|N|140|31|50.23|E|}}) * '''Yakushidō''' – Located to the upper left of the main shrine building, also known as Hisu Shrine; dedicated to Yakushi Nyorai. ({{Coord|40|18|51.39|N|140|31|50.11|E|}}) * '''Yama Shrine''' – A small shrine dedicated to the mountain deity located to the right of the main building; proceeding around it leads to the source of Fudō-no-Taki. ({{Coord|40|18|52.87|N|140|31|50.84|E|}}) * '''Iwaya Jūimen Kannon''' – From the middle of the Cedar Alley, a side path leads to a large rock cave at the foot of the mountain, enshrining the Eleven-Faced Kannon. ({{Coord|40|18|50.03|N|140|31|57.18|E|}}) * '''Shiroiwa''' – A sheer white rock cliff to the left of the cave. * '''Tenjin no Iwa''' – A rock on the northern peak where ancient pines and other trees grow, known as Tenjin Rock. * '''Higashi Nozoki Iwa (Eastern Lookout Rock)''' – A massive rock jutting out to provide a view of the eastern sky. ({{Coord|40|18|59.12|N|140|31|46.83|E|}}) * '''Kagami Iwa''' – A rock that stands like a mirror; also referred to as Eboshi Iwa, due to its unusual shape. ({{Coord|40|18|59.18|N|140|31|46.67|E|}}) * '''Tainai Kugu (Inner Womb Cave)''' – A cave-like opening in the rock, said to evoke the feeling of being within a mother’s womb. ({{Coord|40|18|59.08|N|140|31|46.21|E|}}) * '''Hokoku Iwa''' – Located north of Tainai Kugu near the resting area; recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Nozoki Iwa” or “Byōbu Iwa,” where a “nozoki shugyō” similar to that of Ōmine-san was practiced. ({{Coord|40|18|59.58|N|140|31|43.35|E|}}) * '''Kyūjō''' – Near the summit, a slightly flat resting area where a triangular survey marker once stood. * '''Kineiwa''' – To the west of the resting area, a rock resembling a mortar carried by a moon rabbit. (Currently obscured by trees; on the western slope.) * '''Okunoin''' – Stairs on the western side of the resting area leading to an inner sanctuary called Okunoin (recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Oku no Goza”). From here, ancient features such as the Goma steps, a Zazen stone, and the rock of Gongen were once noted, though they are no longer identifiable. * '''Suzuri Iwa''' – Descending from the summit toward the south, a rock with a concave bottom that always contains water, known as Kōbō’s inkstone. (Near Ōiwa on a neighboring southeastern peak; now obscured by vegetation.) * '''Kengami Mine''' – A sharp rock outcrop with little foothold, described by Sugae Masumi as “Kengamine.” ({{Coord|40|18|42.71|N|140|31|49.76|E|}}) * '''Tengu Iwa''' – The large rocks on Kengami Mine are called Tengu Rock, with the larger one known as Great Tengu and the smaller as Little Tengu. (As recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Daitengu, Shōtengu no Iwa”.) * '''Hasami Iwa''' – Rocks facing each other resembling scissors; encountered along a small, relatively flat path obstructed by a large rock. ({{Coord|40|18|39.93|N|140|31|49.45|E|}}) * '''Tengu-bashi''' – Also known as the Tengu Suspension Bridge, it is the most scenic spot on the mountain. A massive rock bridges a deep chasm; crossing it offers a daunting view below. (Recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Daitengu no Tsuri-bashi.”) ({{Coord|40|18|37.95|N|140|31|51.35|E|}}) * '''Tsuzumi Iwa''' – A flat rock encountered when descending from Tengu Iwa, which produces a drum-like sound when stepped upon. (Recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Kago Iwa” and also as Tsuzumi Iwa.) ({{Coord|40|18|34.86|N|140|31|51.11|E|}}) After descending from Tsuzumi Iwa and turning left, one emerges below the First Torii and reaches the original road.<ref>『釈迦内郷土誌』, Shakani Kominkan, pp.265–269, composed during the Taishō era and reprinted in Heisei 1.</ref> == Sankokuga (Three-hooked Bell) == Sankokuga is an ancient bell excavated from Matsumine-san, which was presented to the Satake clan during the Edo period and is now housed in the [[:en:Tokyo National Museum|Tokyo National Museum]]. A receipt document from the Satake clan is recorded in the "Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi," and the "Hu Yin Onko-shi" confirms its existence. Locally, it is known as the "Station Bell" (Ekiro no Suzu). When [[Hitomi Shōu]] visited the region in 1797 (Kansei 9), he remarked that he had only heard of the Station Bell, and later Nikaidō Shokushima, in 1800 (Kansei 12), witnessed it and noted that it was housed at Seitōin in Kashima District or belonged to Matsumine-san in Dewa Akita-gun. He mentioned that it was unearthed in Tanaka about 100 years ago, and an elderly man from western regions confirmed that it was essentially identical to the bell from Kashima, hence the name "Station Bell" became established.<ref name="hinai"/> There is also a scholarly paper titled "On the Ancient Bell Housed by the Satake Family" discussing its true nature, though no definitive conclusion has been reached. This bell was transferred from the Satake family between April 24 and May 16, 1999 (Heisei 11) to the Tokyo National Museum, and was exhibited in the "Sankokuga Homecoming Exhibition" at the Ōdate Local Museum. According to some records in the "Kubota-gun Eki-ki," "Akita Fudoki," and "Gyōson Shiryaku," the bell was buried due to an earthquake, and an iron alligator was also excavated alongside it.<ref name="hinai"/> == Denjuin == Denjuin is recorded as the local temple of Matsumine-san. Sugae Masumi left an illustration of Denjuin, depicting it to the left of the First Torii when viewed from the base of the mountain. By the time the "Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi" was compiled, Denjuin had already been abolished. In [[:en:1598|1598 AD]], when the Asari clan perished and Ōdate came under the control of Akita Miki, Denjuin received a total of 70 shaku from the Akita clan. This indicates that Matsumine-san had been widely venerated in the Hinai region since the Asari era or earlier, independent of the Asari clan. During the Edo period, documents record that the Satake clan of Ōdate provided 9 shaku and two retinues.<ref name="hinai"/> == Fudō-dō == Fudō-dō is the main shrine building of Matsumine-san. According to records in the "Kubota-gun Eki-ki," "Akita Fudoki," and "Gyōson Shiryaku," it burned down in [[:en:1786|1786 AD]] (Tenmei 6). According to a document titled "Shoshokurichū-chō," Fudō-dō also burned down on the night of April 8, 1863 (Bunkyū 3) due to a fire, resulting in the loss of the Fudō statue, and the local Denjuin was ordered by the Satake clan to observe 50 days of mourning. Fudō-dō was reconstructed in [[:en:1867|1867 AD]] (Keiō 3). Timber was felled from within Matsumine-san, and contributions were solicited from the surrounding area. However, in 1868 (Keiō 4, Meiji 1), during the Akita War when Ōdate City was burned and amid the anti-Buddhist ([[:en:Haibutsu kishaku|Haibutsu kishaku]]) movement, although contributions of 180 ryo were collected at the time of reconstruction, by the time of the Fudō-dō relocation in 1871 only 1 ryo 2 bu was raised, indicating severe economic hardship.<ref name="hinai"/> Once a [[:en:Shingon Buddhism|Shingon sect]] temple known as Matsumine-san, it was later converted to a shrine in accordance with the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, with the principal deity changed to {{ill|Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|lt=Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|lt=Tsukuyomi|ja|月夜見命|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuyomi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ツクヨミ}}, and the name was changed to Matsumine Shrine. == Yakushi Shrine == Yakushi Shrine, also known as Hisu Shrine, is located on a small rise to the left of the main shrine building. It enshrines two statues of Yakushi Nyorai, which were donated in the Shōho Besshoku year (【1646 AD】) and in the Hōreki 10th year (【1760 AD】). In addition, many small stones with holes or inscribed with “me” are offered. A spring known as "Yakusui" is found midway up the steps; it is customary to purify one’s eyes with this water.<ref name="matu"/> == Tengu-sama == Among the many giant cedar and pine trees on Matsumine-san, one particularly distinctive giant cedar, known locally as the "Tengu Cedar," was reputed to have a hollow interior that served as the dwelling of tengu. However, as the tree died, it was cut down in Taishō 6, and the felled trunk was donated to Matsumine Shrine as a memorial. It is estimated to have had a diameter of nearly 3 m. During the Pacific War, families of soldiers—especially those whose relatives served in aviation units—visited the shrine and offered white and red paper fans in the hope of emulating the tengu’s ability to fly freely. It was also widely visited by families for protection against enemy bullets, due to the tengu’s reputed supernatural powers.<ref name="matu"/> == Suijin Shrine == Suijin Shrine is a small stone shrine located to the right, just before the stone steps. Known as Wakami, it is said that drinking water from here will restore youth; this tradition continues today on New Year’s Day.<ref name="matu"/> == Gosai == Gosai is a commemorative monument located to the left of the stone steps. There are no other monuments of its kind in Akita Prefecture. It is attributed to Emperor Uda. ({{Coord|40|18|51.82|N|140|31|51.31|E|}}) == Inari Shrine == The village shrine (satoyama) of Matsumine Shrine is an Inari Shrine, currently located in the western part of the Matsumine settlement ({{Coord|40|18|25.3|N|140|32|47.27|E|}}). Its enshrined deities are {{ill|Kura Inadama no Mikoto|ja|倉稲魂神|1=Ukanomitama|2=ja|3=倉稲魂神|4=de|5=Ukanomitama|6=eo|7=Ukanomitama|8=mni|9=ꯎꯀꯅꯣꯃꯤꯇꯃ|10=ru|11=Ука-но_митама|12=simple|13=Ukanomitama|14=sv|15=Ukanomitama|16=zh|17=宇迦之御魂神|lt=Ukanomitama|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kura Inadama no Mikoto|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ウカノミタマ}}, {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|lt=Sarutahiko Ōkami|lt=Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to サルタヒコ}}, and {{ill|Ōmiya-uru no Mikoto|ja|大宮売命|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōmiya-uru no Mikoto|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to オオミヤノメ|1=Ōmiyanome|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24865597}}. Its festival is held every October 10. Within its precincts there are monuments such as a stele of Sarutahiko, a “Twenty-Three Night Stele” (also known as Tsukimai-to), and a stone monument featuring a horse head.<ref name="matu"/> At the Inari Shrine, there are three dolls made of straw and pampas grass, with a history of approximately 450 years. Every last Sunday in November, the Matsumine settlement holds a doll festival. According to tradition, about 800 years ago, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshitsune|Minamoto no Yoshitsune]], accompanied by [[:en:Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] and [[:en:Nasu no Yoichi|Nasu no Yoichi]], passed through this area, inspiring the local people to create dolls out of reverence. These dolls were originally placed at the three entrances to the settlement to ward off epidemics and evil spirits, and were later enshrined within the Inari Shrine during the early Taishō period.<ref>「広報おおだて」, Shōwa 61, April 16</ref> == Records by Sugae Masumi and the Matumine-san Faith Sites == In June 1803 (Kyōwa 3), Sugae Masumi visited Matsumine-san and recorded his impressions in "Nie Nō Jikagarami." He noted, "On April 8, when a ceremony is held, many people come to worship at the main shrine. In the old days, those local Upase people who had not yet ascended to Nara’s Ōmine or Katsuragi would chant 'sange sange' and adorn themselves with prayer beads, bells, headscarves, and ayahikasa, carrying a dango-staff along with a spiral staff and a scepter, as they entered this peak." == Yamada Keizō == Marathon runner Yamada Keizō, from Ōdate City, who won the Boston Marathon in 1953 with a world record time, practiced running up and down the stone steps of Matsumine Shrine in his youth.<ref>Ōdate City, “Shakani Fieldwork – Matsumine Shrine Edition” [https://common3.pref.akita.lg.jp/genkimura/blog/?p=45876]</ref> == Matsumine Settlement and Matsumine Mine == The Matsumine Settlement, formerly known as Tanaka Village, was located at the confluence of the Shimonakagawa and Hanaokagawa rivers, about 300 m from the village. In 1963, a black ore deposit extending approximately 3000 mt was discovered 250–300 m underground beneath the settlement. Due to mining, subsidence occurred, and by 1976, 85 households were collectively relocated to the present site. In 1973, Matsumine Station was opened in the vicinity. Matsumine Mine extracted black ore from the Ōyama ore deposit using an open-column (open-pit) method. In 1932, its annual output surpassed that of the Ashio Copper Mine, and in 1970 it achieved a national record of 16,285 t per year. In 1979, despite aging facilities and maintenance expenses, soaring metal prices led to high revenues of 2.28 billion yen. However, due to a downturn in metal prices, the mine was closed in 1994 (Heisei 6), while leaving some reserves intact. During the Taishō period, this area suffered from severe smog caused by emissions from Kosaka Mine and Hanaoka Mine; the Matsumine area was the worst affected. Matsumine-san suffered greatly, with all its pine and chestnut trees dying, and in 1915 (Taishō 4) the entire mountain was deforested, leading to extensive reforestation. The history of this event is detailed on a commemorative monument by the shrine's stone steps.<ref name="matu"/> == Ōyama == {{Infobox mountain |Name = Ōyama |image = [[File:Ôyama(Ôdate si).jpg|250px]] |image Caption = Ōyama in Ōdate City (Matsumine-san) |Elevation = 375.6 m |Coordinates = {{coord|40|18|52.9|N|140|31|43.2|E|type:mountain_region:JP|display=inline}} |Location = {{JPN}}<br />[[:en:Akita Prefecture|Akita Prefecture]], [[:en:Ōdate|Ōdate City]], Matsumine Ōyama |Mountain Range = |Type = |First Ascent = |Map = {{Location map|Japan Akita Prefecture#Japan|relief=1|float=center}}{{日本の位置情報|40|18|53.05|140|31|43.2|Ōyama|40.314737,140.528669|Ōyama|nocoord=yes}} }} The highest peak of Matsumine-san is Ōyama (375.7 m), which epitomizes the very notion of a "mountain." On Ōyama, there is a pine known as the "Makka Pine," which, upon reaching 62 years of age, is said to be designated as such. Additionally, unusually for a mountain of roughly 300 m class, about 100 native [[:en:Fagus crenata|Buna]] trees grow here<ref name="matu"/>. Although the number of trees is small, Ōyama is home to many rare and endangered plant species, including [[:en:Arisaema thunbergii subsp. urashima|Urashima-sō]], {{ill|Shōjōbakama|ja|ショウジョウバカマ|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōjōbakama|qq=|1=Heloniopsis orientalis|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7338626}}, [[:en:Lilium medeoloides|Kuramayuri]], [[:en:Epigaea asiatica|Iwanashi]], {{ill|Yamazaki-sō|ja|ヤマザキソウ|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamazaki-sō|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, [[:en:Cymbidium goeringii|Shunran]], {{ill|Kakiran|ja|カキラン|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kakiran|qq=|1=Epipactis thunbergii|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q5978054}}, [[:en:Cephalanthera erecta|Ginran]], {{ill|Ruiyōbotan|ja|ルイヨウボタン|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ruiyōbotan|qq=|1=Caulophyllum robustum|comment=changed title based on Bamanasaku|ja|アカバナマルバマンサク|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Akabanamaru Bamanasaku|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and [[:en:Cypripedium japonicum|Kumagaisho]], among others.<ref '''Matumine Shrine''' ({{ill|Matumine Shrine|ja|松峰神社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matumine Shrine|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) is a Shinto shrine located in Matsumine, Oyamagai, Ōdate City, [[:en:Akita Prefecture|Akita Prefecture]].
'''Matumine-san Faith Sites''' ({{ill|Matumine-san Shinkō Iseki-gun|ja|松峰山信仰遺跡群|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matumine-san Shinkō Iseki-gun|qq=|1=Ō Yama|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q67587030}}) refers to the group of ancient and medieval esoteric ([[:en:Mikkyō|Mikkyo]]) sites associated with auspicious legends that cluster around Matumine Shrine. The mountain, named after the honzon of the shrine—[[:en:Acala|Fudō Myōō]] of the former Ryouakkosan Dainenji—has its central peak, Ōyama, at an elevation of 375.7 m. The village shrine (satoyama) located at 141-5, Nioida, Ōdate City, is now known as the Matsumine [[:en:Inari shrine|Inari Shrine]]. Matumine-san Faith Sites were designated as a historic site by Ōdate City on May 1, 2009 (Heisei 21), with coordinates based on the designated cultural property map. During the Edo period, it was known as "Matsumine Kureyuki" in the Eight Views of Ōdate and served as the 32nd sacred site in the Akita Rokugun Sanjū Sankannon Reijō.
== Legend == The honzon of Matumine Shrine is Fudō Myōō (attributed to the works of {{ill|Kōbō Daishi|ja|弘法大師|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōbō Daishi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海|1=Kūkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q222227}}) accompanied by two guardian child deities.
== Enshrined Deities and Subsidiary Shrines == * Honzon: Fudō Myōō (伝弘法大師作) and two guardian child deities (Zenritsu Nīdōji) * Subsidiary shrines include: Yakushidō, the mountain deity shrine, Uga Shrine, Kurikara Fudō Taki (whose waterfall becomes Haragawa), Iwaya Jūimen Kannon (attributed to Kōbō Daishi), and Shō Kannon (attributed to Senchō).
== History == In [[:en:817|817 AD]] (Kōnin 8), {{ill|Kōbō Daishi|ja|弘法大師|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōbō Daishi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海|1=Kūkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q222227}} is said to have founded the mountain. He cast a bronze statue of Amida Kannon and made a mirror out of silver, naming it Daienkō. In [[:en:822|822 AD]] (Kōnin 13), the Left Minister Seikō-shaden was constructed. In March [[:en:857|857 AD]] (Tennan 1), an earthquake buried all existing structures. In [[:en:891|891 AD]] (Kanpei 3), Emperor Uda granted a headband to Ono Yoshimitsu, the son of Ono Yoshiya (father of Ono Komachi). That same year, a manuscript inscribed with “Yamashi no Hikari mo Toki ni Umamaruru, Araware Terase Matsumine no Tsuki” was presented. In [[:en:895|895 AD]] (Kanpei 7), Ono Yoshifusa was appointed as the official, and the shrine building was constructed.
Afterwards, the subsequent history remains obscure for several centuries. In [[:en:1403|1403 AD]] (Ōei 10), the local lord of the {{ill|Asari clan|ja|浅利氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Asari clan|qq=|1=Asari clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11557021}} began to revere the shrine, and in the first year of Kei'an the Satake clan, devotees of Fudō, transformed the main shrine into a Buddhist temple hall. During the Kansei era, a monk from Denshūin discovered a bell in the soil. In [[:en:1801|1801 AD]] (Kyōwa 1), the feudal lord Satake Yoshikazu presented this bell during a tour of his domain. In the 3rd year of the Meiji era, the Buddhist Fudō was abolished. For the regular festivals, items from the former domain were provided. In [[:en:1873|1873 AD]] (Meiji 6), the shrine was reclassified as a village shrine. The current enshrined deity is {{ill|Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|lt=Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|lt=Tsukuyomi|ja|月読大神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuyomi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. The main shrine building was formerly known as Furuta Nakamura, but it later adopted the name Matsumine Shrine, after the mountain on which it stands.<ref>『釈迦内郷土誌』, Shakani Kominkan, pp.93–95</ref>
The komainu at the main shrine were donated by {{ill|Itahabutakesuke|ja|伊多波武助|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Itahabutakesuke|qq=|1=Itaba Busuke|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24861288}}.<ref>『秋田ふしぎ探訪』, Mumyōsha Publishing, 1979</ref>
== “Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi” == Numerous ancient texts record the legends of Matsumine-san. Representative texts include: * ''Akita Rokugun Sanjū Sankannon Junrei-ki''<ref>Kyōhō era (1716–1736), [{{NDLDC|1174121/16}}] in Akita Sōsho Vol.8 and in Shin Akita Sōsho Vol.3</ref> * ''Kubota-gun Eki-ki'' * ''Akita Fudoki'' * ''Gyōson Shiryaku'' * “Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi”<ref name="hinai">『大館郷土博物館研究紀要 火内』 Vol.12, March 2015, pp.13–29, “Materials on Matsumine-san Faith,” from the Matsumine-san Shinkō Iseki-gun Examination Subcommittee of the Ōdate City Cultural Property Protection Council</ref>
Other notable features on Matsumine-san include: * '''Haragawa''' – A small stream flowing from the waterfall of Fudō located on the right side below the stone steps of the approach. The waterfall is so named because it is used to wash away impurities from worshipers. ({{Coord|40|18|43.02|N|140|32|48.01|E|}}) * '''Shinmeisha''' – A small shrine on a hill about one chō (approximately 100 m) from the foot of the mountain; also called O-Ise-sama. ({{Coord|40|18|50.71|N|140|32|31.59|E|}}) * '''Yuden-yama''' – A distant monument to Yuden-yama, established in [[:en:1770|1770 AD]]. ({{Coord|40|18|48.76|N|140|32|35.53|E|}}) * '''Kōshin-zuka''' – A mound established in [[:en:1778|1778 AD]]. ({{Coord|40|18|48.61|N|140|32|34.72|E|}}) * '''Okoishi and Obaishi''' – Stones enshrining [[:en:Manjushri|Manjushri]] and [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Fugen Bosatsu]]. ({{Coord|40|18|54.11|N|140|32|20.70|E|}}) and ({{Coord|40|18|54.73|N|140|32|19.62|E|}}) * '''Yenaki Iwa''' – A stone said to have the power to silence a crying child. ({{Coord|40|18|54.42|N|140|32|10.97|E|}}) * '''Usa Shrine''' – A small shrine near the first torii where a small grass sickle is offered to cure smallpox in children. ({{Coord|40|18|53.77|N|140|32|04.32|E|}}) * '''The First Torii''' – A large stone torii; historically, a pond and garden existed to its right. ({{Coord|40|18|54.02|N|140|31|59.77|E|}}) * '''Denjuin''' – As recorded by Sugae Masumi, an illustration depicts Denjuin to the left of the first torii. This structure once existed between the first torii and the former pond and is said to mark the beginning of the mountain climbing route.<ref name="meisyo">“Matsumine Mountain Scenic Tour Association” (record, June 16, Heisei 3) by the Matsumine Town Association</ref> * '''Cedar Alley''' – A row of giant cedars between the first torii and the main shrine building. Although not mentioned in Sugae Masumi’s writings, old maps clearly depict it. Currently, the largest cedar is approximately 6.5 m in circumference and is over 600 years old. ({{Coord|40|18|53.18|N|140|31|56.64|E|}}) * '''Stone Steps''' – Approximately 170 stone steps (commonly stated as 160), also known as “Ishinokizahashi.”<ref name="matu"/> * '''Fudō-no-Taki''' – The waterfall of Fudō on the right side of the stone steps, whose water flows from a sheer cliff and eventually becomes Haragawa. Worshipers use it for purification before ascending to the main shrine. ({{Coord|40|18|52.91|N|140|31|53.66|E|}}) * '''Uga Shrine''' – A small stone shrine located to the right, along the waterfall’s flow, known as Uga no Kami; it is also called the small water shrine of Uga. ({{Coord|40|18|52.91|N|140|31|53.66|E|}}) * '''Main Shrine Building''' – The shrine grounds cover an area of 6 tan 11 bu, and the current main building was constructed by Satake Yoshinori starting in Meiji 3 and completed in April of Meiji 4. ({{Coord|40|18|52.23|N|140|31|50.23|E|}}) * '''Yakushidō''' – Located to the upper left of the main shrine building, also known as Hisu Shrine; dedicated to Yakushi Nyorai. ({{Coord|40|18|51.39|N|140|31|50.11|E|}}) * '''Yama Shrine''' – A small shrine dedicated to the mountain deity located to the right of the main building; proceeding around it leads to the source of Fudō-no-Taki. ({{Coord|40|18|52.87|N|140|31|50.84|E|}}) * '''Iwaya Jūimen Kannon''' – From the middle of the Cedar Alley, a side path leads to a large rock cave at the foot of the mountain, enshrining the Eleven-Faced Kannon. ({{Coord|40|18|50.03|N|140|31|57.18|E|}}) * '''Shiroiwa''' – A sheer white rock cliff to the left of the cave. * '''Tenjin no Iwa''' – A rock on the northern peak where ancient pines and other trees grow, known as Tenjin Rock. * '''Higashi Nozoki Iwa (Eastern Lookout Rock)''' – A massive rock jutting out to provide a view of the eastern sky. ({{Coord|40|18|59.12|N|140|31|46.83|E|}}) * '''Kagami Iwa''' – A rock that stands like a mirror; also referred to as Eboshi Iwa, due to its unusual shape. ({{Coord|40|18|59.18|N|140|31|46.67|E|}}) * '''Tainai Kugu (Inner Womb Cave)''' – A cave-like opening in the rock, said to evoke the feeling of being within a mother’s womb. ({{Coord|40|18|59.08|N|140|31|46.21|E|}}) * '''Hokoku Iwa''' – Located north of Tainai Kugu near the resting area; recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Nozoki Iwa” or “Byōbu Iwa,” where a “nozoki shugyō” similar to that of Ōmine-san was practiced. ({{Coord|40|18|59.58|N|140|31|43.35|E|}}) * '''Kyūjō''' – Near the summit, a slightly flat resting area where a triangular survey marker once stood. * '''Kineiwa''' – To the west of the resting area, a rock resembling a mortar carried by a moon rabbit. (Currently obscured by trees; on the western slope.) * '''Okunoin''' – Stairs on the western side of the resting area leading to an inner sanctuary called Okunoin (recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Oku no Goza”). From here, ancient features such as the Goma steps, a Zazen stone, and the rock of Gongen were once noted, though they are no longer identifiable. * '''Suzuri Iwa''' – Descending from the summit toward the south, a rock with a concave bottom that always contains water, known as Kōbō’s inkstone. (Near Ōiwa on a neighboring southeastern peak; now obscured by vegetation.) * '''Kengami Mine''' – A sharp rock outcrop with little foothold, described by Sugae Masumi as “Kengamine.” ({{Coord|40|18|42.71|N|140|31|49.76|E|}}) * '''Tengu Iwa''' – The large rocks on Kengami Mine are called Tengu Rock, with the larger one known as Great Tengu and the smaller as Little Tengu. (As recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Daitengu, Shōtengu no Iwa”.) * '''Hasami Iwa''' – Rocks facing each other resembling scissors; encountered along a small, relatively flat path obstructed by a large rock. ({{Coord|40|18|39.93|N|140|31|49.45|E|}}) * '''Tengu-bashi''' – Also known as the Tengu Suspension Bridge, it is the most scenic spot on the mountain. A massive rock bridges a deep chasm; crossing it offers a daunting view below. (Recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Daitengu no Tsuri-bashi.”) ({{Coord|40|18|37.95|N|140|31|51.35|E|}}) * '''Tsuzumi Iwa''' – A flat rock encountered when descending from Tengu Iwa, which produces a drum-like sound when stepped upon. (Recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Kago Iwa” and also as Tsuzumi Iwa.) ({{Coord|40|18|34.86|N|140|31|51.11|E|}}) After descending from Tsuzumi Iwa and turning left, one emerges below the First Torii and reaches the original road.<ref>『釈迦内郷土誌』, Shakani Kominkan, pp.265–269, composed during the Taishō era and reprinted in Heisei 1.</ref> == Sankokuga (Three-hooked Bell) == Sankokuga is an ancient bell excavated from Matsumine-san, which was presented to the Satake clan during the Edo period and is now housed in the [[:en:Tokyo National Museum|Tokyo National Museum]]. A receipt document from the Satake clan is recorded in the "Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi," and the "Hu Yin Onko-shi" confirms its existence. Locally, it is known as the "Station Bell" (Ekiro no Suzu). When [[Hitomi Shōu]] visited the region in 1797 (Kansei 9), he remarked that he had only heard of the Station Bell, and later Nikaidō Shokushima, in 1800 (Kansei 12), witnessed it and noted that it was housed at Seitōin in Kashima District or belonged to Matsumine-san in Dewa Akita-gun. He mentioned that it was unearthed in Tanaka about 100 years ago, and an elderly man from western regions confirmed that it was essentially identical to the bell from Kashima, hence the name "Station Bell" became established.<ref name="hinai"/> There is also a scholarly paper titled "On the Ancient Bell Housed by the Satake Family" discussing its true nature, though no definitive conclusion has been reached. This bell was transferred from the Satake family between April 24 and May 16, 1999 (Heisei 11) to the Tokyo National Museum, and was exhibited in the "Sankokuga Homecoming Exhibition" at the Ōdate Local Museum. According to some records in the "Kubota-gun Eki-ki," "Akita Fudoki," and "Gyōson Shiryaku," the bell was buried due to an earthquake, and an iron alligator was also excavated alongside it.<ref name="hinai"/> == Denjuin == Denjuin is recorded as the local temple of Matsumine-san. Sugae Masumi left an illustration of Denjuin, depicting it to the left of the First Torii when viewed from the base of the mountain. By the time the "Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi" was compiled, Denjuin had already been abolished. In [[:en:1598|1598 AD]], when the Asari clan perished and Ōdate came under the control of Akita Miki, Denjuin received a total of 70 shaku from the Akita clan. This indicates that Matsumine-san had been widely venerated in the Hinai region since the Asari era or earlier, independent of the Asari clan. During the Edo period, documents record that the Satake clan of Ōdate provided 9 shaku and two retinues.<ref name="hinai"/> == Fudō-dō == Fudō-dō is the main shrine building of Matsumine-san. According to records in the "Kubota-gun Eki-ki," "Akita Fudoki," and "Gyōson Shiryaku," it burned down in [[:en:1786|1786 AD]] (Tenmei 6). According to a document titled "Shoshokurichū-chō," Fudō-dō also burned down on the night of April 8, 1863 (Bunkyū 3) due to a fire, resulting in the loss of the Fudō statue, and the local Denjuin was ordered by the Satake clan to observe 50 days of mourning. Fudō-dō was reconstructed in [[:en:1867|1867 AD]] (Keiō 3). Timber was felled from within Matsumine-san, and contributions were solicited from the surrounding area. However, in 1868 (Keiō 4, Meiji 1), during the Akita War when Ōdate City was burned and amid the anti-Buddhist ([[:en:Haibutsu kishaku|Haibutsu kishaku]]) movement, although contributions of 180 ryo were collected at the time of reconstruction, by the time of the Fudō-dō relocation in 1871 only 1 ryo 2 bu was raised, indicating severe economic hardship.<ref name="hinai"/> Once a [[:en:Shingon Buddhism|Shingon sect]] temple known as Matsumine-san, it was later converted to a shrine in accordance with the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, with the principal deity changed to {{ill|Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|lt=Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|lt=Tsukuyomi|ja|月夜見命|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuyomi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ツクヨミ}}, and the name was changed to Matsumine Shrine. == Yakushi Shrine == Yakushi Shrine, also known as Hisu Shrine, is located on a small rise to the left of the main shrine building. It enshrines two statues of Yakushi Nyorai, which were donated in the Shōho Besshoku year (【1646 AD】) and in the Hōreki 10th year (【1760 AD】). In addition, many small stones with holes or inscribed with “me” are offered. A spring known as "Yakusui" is found midway up the steps; it is customary to purify one’s eyes with this water.<ref name="matu"/> == Tengu-sama == Among the many giant cedar and pine trees on Matsumine-san, one particularly distinctive giant cedar, known locally as the "Tengu Cedar," was reputed to have a hollow interior that served as the dwelling of tengu. However, as the tree died, it was cut down in Taishō 6, and the felled trunk was donated to Matsumine Shrine as a memorial. It is estimated to have had a diameter of nearly 3 m. During the Pacific War, families of soldiers—especially those whose relatives served in aviation units—visited the shrine and offered white and red paper fans in the hope of emulating the tengu’s ability to fly freely. It was also widely visited by families for protection against enemy bullets, due to the tengu’s reputed supernatural powers.<ref name="matu"/> == Suijin Shrine == Suijin Shrine is a small stone shrine located to the right, just before the stone steps. Known as Wakami, it is said that drinking water from here will restore youth; this tradition continues today on New Year’s Day.<ref name="matu"/> == Gosai == Gosai is a commemorative monument located to the left of the stone steps. There are no other monuments of its kind in Akita Prefecture. It is attributed to Emperor Uda. ({{Coord|40|18|51.82|N|140|31|51.31|E|}}) == Inari Shrine == The village shrine (satoyama) of Matsumine Shrine is an Inari Shrine, currently located in the western part of the Matsumine settlement ({{Coord|40|18|25.3|N|140|32|47.27|E|}}). Its enshrined deities are {{ill|Kura Inadama no Mikoto|ja|倉稲魂神|1=Ukanomitama|2=ja|3=倉稲魂神|4=de|5=Ukanomitama|6=eo|7=Ukanomitama|8=mni|9=ꯎꯀꯅꯣꯃꯤꯇꯃ|10=ru|11=Ука-но_митама|12=simple|13=Ukanomitama|14=sv|15=Ukanomitama|16=zh|17=宇迦之御魂神|lt=Ukanomitama|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kura Inadama no Mikoto|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ウカノミタマ}}, {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|lt=Sarutahiko Ōkami|lt=Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to サルタヒコ}}, and {{ill|Ōmiya-uru no Mikoto|ja|大宮売命|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōmiya-uru no Mikoto|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to オオミヤノメ|1=Ōmiyanome|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24865597}}. Its festival is held every October 10. Within its precincts there are monuments such as a stele of Sarutahiko, a “Twenty-Three Night Stele” (also known as Tsukimai-to), and a stone monument featuring a horse head.<ref name="matu"/> At the Inari Shrine, there are three dolls made of straw and pampas grass, with a history of approximately 450 years. Every last Sunday in November, the Matsumine settlement holds a doll festival. According to tradition, about 800 years ago, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshitsune|Minamoto no Yoshitsune]], accompanied by [[:en:Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] and [[:en:Nasu no Yoichi|Nasu no Yoichi]], passed through this area, inspiring the local people to create dolls out of reverence. These dolls were originally placed at the three entrances to the settlement to ward off epidemics and evil spirits, and were later enshrined within the Inari Shrine during the early Taishō period.<ref>「広報おおだて」, Shōwa 61, April 16</ref> == Records by Sugae Masumi and the Matumine-san Faith Sites == In June 1803 (Kyōwa 3), Sugae Masumi visited Matsumine-san and recorded his impressions in "Nie Nō Jikagarami." He noted, "On April 8, when a ceremony is held, many people come to worship at the main shrine. In the old days, those local Upase people who had not yet ascended to Nara’s Ōmine or Katsuragi would chant 'sange sange' and adorn themselves with prayer beads, bells, headscarves, and ayahikasa, carrying a dango-staff along with a spiral staff and a scepter, as they entered this peak." == Yamada Keizō == Marathon runner Yamada Keizō, from Ōdate City, who won the Boston Marathon in 1953 with a world record time, practiced running up and down the stone steps of Matsumine Shrine in his youth.<ref>Ōdate City, “Shakani Fieldwork – Matsumine Shrine Edition” [https://common3.pref.akita.lg.jp/genkimura/blog/?p=45876]</ref> == Matsumine Settlement and Matsumine Mine == The Matsumine Settlement, formerly known as Tanaka Village, was located at the confluence of the Shimonakagawa and Hanaokagawa rivers, about 300 m from the village. In 1963, a black ore deposit extending approximately 3000 mt was discovered 250–300 m underground beneath the settlement. Due to mining, subsidence occurred, and by 1976, 85 households were collectively relocated to the present site. In 1973, Matsumine Station was opened in the vicinity. Matsumine Mine extracted black ore from the Ōyama ore deposit using an open-column (open-pit) method. In 1932, its annual output surpassed that of the Ashio Copper Mine, and in 1970 it achieved a national record of 16,285 t per year. In 1979, despite aging facilities and maintenance expenses, soaring metal prices led to high revenues of 2.28 billion yen. However, due to a downturn in metal prices, the mine was closed in 1994 (Heisei 6), while leaving some reserves intact. During the Taishō period, this area suffered from severe smog caused by emissions from Kosaka Mine and Hanaoka Mine; the Matsumine area was the worst affected. Matsumine-san suffered greatly, with all its pine and chestnut trees dying, and in 1915 (Taishō 4) the entire mountain was deforested, leading to extensive reforestation. The history of this event is detailed on a commemorative monument by the shrine's stone steps.<ref name="matu"/> == Ōyama == {{Infobox mountain |Name = Ōyama |image = [[File:Ôyama(Ôdate si).jpg|250px]] |image Caption = Ōyama in Ōdate City (Matsumine-san) |Elevation = 375.6 m |Coordinates = {{coord|40|18|52.9|N|140|31|43.2|E|type:mountain_region:JP|display=inline}} |Location = {{JPN}}<br />[[:en:Akita Prefecture|Akita Prefecture]], [[:en:Ōdate|Ōdate City]], Matsumine Ōyama |Mountain Range = |Type = |First Ascent = |Map = {{Location map|Japan Akita Prefecture#Japan|relief=1|float=center}}{{日本の位置情報|40|18|53.05|140|31|43.2|Ōyama|40.314737,140.528669|Ōyama|nocoord=yes}} }} The highest peak of Matsumine-san is Ōyama (375.7 m), which epitomizes the very notion of a "mountain." On Ōyama, there is a pine known as the "Makka Pine," which, upon reaching 62 years of age, is said to be designated as such. Additionally, unusually for a mountain of roughly 300 m class, about 100 native [[:en:Fagus crenata|Buna]] trees grow here<ref name="matu"/>. Although the number of trees is small, Ōyama is home to many rare and endangered plant species, including [[:en:Arisaema thunbergii subsp. urashima|Urashima-sō]], '''Matumine Shrine''' ({{ill|Matumine Shrine|ja|松峰神社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matumine Shrine|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) is a Shinto shrine located in Matsumine, Oyamagai, Ōdate City, [[:en:Akita Prefecture|Akita Prefecture]].
'''Matumine-san Faith Sites''' ({{ill|Matumine-san Shinkō Iseki-gun|ja|松峰山信仰遺跡群|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matumine-san Shinkō Iseki-gun|qq=|1=Ō Yama|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q67587030}}) refers to the group of ancient and medieval esoteric ([[:en:Mikkyō|Mikkyo]]) sites associated with auspicious legends that cluster around Matumine Shrine. The mountain, named after the honzon of the shrine—[[:en:Acala|Fudō Myōō]] of the former Ryouakkosan Dainenji—has its central peak, Ōyama, at an elevation of 375.7 m. The village shrine (satoyama) located at 141-5, Nioida, Ōdate City, is now known as the Matsumine [[:en:Inari shrine|Inari Shrine]]. Matumine-san Faith Sites were designated as a historic site by Ōdate City on May 1, 2009 (Heisei 21), with coordinates based on the designated cultural property map. During the Edo period, it was known as "Matsumine Kureyuki" in the Eight Views of Ōdate and served as the 32nd sacred site in the Akita Rokugun Sanjū Sankannon Reijō.
== Legend == The honzon of Matumine Shrine is Fudō Myōō (attributed to the works of {{ill|Kōbō Daishi|ja|弘法大師|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōbō Daishi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海|1=Kūkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q222227}}) accompanied by two guardian child deities.
== Enshrined Deities and Subsidiary Shrines == * Honzon: Fudō Myōō (伝弘法大師作) and two guardian child deities (Zenritsu Nīdōji) * Subsidiary shrines include: Yakushidō, the mountain deity shrine, Uga Shrine, Kurikara Fudō Taki (whose waterfall becomes Haragawa), Iwaya Jūimen Kannon (attributed to Kōbō Daishi), and Shō Kannon (attributed to Senchō).
== History == In [[:en:817|817 AD]] (Kōnin 8), {{ill|Kōbō Daishi|ja|弘法大師|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōbō Daishi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海|1=Kūkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q222227}} is said to have founded the mountain. He cast a bronze statue of Amida Kannon and made a mirror out of silver, naming it Daienkō. In [[:en:822|822 AD]] (Kōnin 13), the Left Minister Seikō-shaden was constructed. In March [[:en:857|857 AD]] (Tennan 1), an earthquake buried all existing structures. In [[:en:891|891 AD]] (Kanpei 3), Emperor Uda granted a headband to Ono Yoshimitsu, the son of Ono Yoshiya (father of Ono Komachi). That same year, a manuscript inscribed with “Yamashi no Hikari mo Toki ni Umamaruru, Araware Terase Matsumine no Tsuki” was presented. In [[:en:895|895 AD]] (Kanpei 7), Ono Yoshifusa was appointed as the official, and the shrine building was constructed.
Afterwards, the subsequent history remains obscure for several centuries. In [[:en:1403|1403 AD]] (Ōei 10), the local lord of the {{ill|Asari clan|ja|浅利氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Asari clan|qq=|1=Asari clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11557021}} began to revere the shrine, and in the first year of Kei'an the Satake clan, devotees of Fudō, transformed the main shrine into a Buddhist temple hall. During the Kansei era, a monk from Denshūin discovered a bell in the soil. In [[:en:1801|1801 AD]] (Kyōwa 1), the feudal lord Satake Yoshikazu presented this bell during a tour of his domain. In the 3rd year of the Meiji era, the Buddhist Fudō was abolished. For the regular festivals, items from the former domain were provided. In [[:en:1873|1873 AD]] (Meiji 6), the shrine was reclassified as a village shrine. The current enshrined deity is {{ill|Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|lt=Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|lt=Tsukuyomi|ja|月読大神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuyomi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. The main shrine building was formerly known as Furuta Nakamura, but it later adopted the name Matsumine Shrine, after the mountain on which it stands.<ref>『釈迦内郷土誌』, Shakani Kominkan, pp.93–95</ref>
The komainu at the main shrine were donated by {{ill|Itahabutakesuke|ja|伊多波武助|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Itahabutakesuke|qq=|1=Itaba Busuke|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24861288}}.<ref>『秋田ふしぎ探訪』, Mumyōsha Publishing, 1979</ref>
== “Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi” == Numerous ancient texts record the legends of Matsumine-san. Representative texts include: * ''Akita Rokugun Sanjū Sankannon Junrei-ki''<ref>Kyōhō era (1716–1736), [{{NDLDC|1174121/16}}] in Akita Sōsho Vol.8 and in Shin Akita Sōsho Vol.3</ref> * ''Kubota-gun Eki-ki'' * ''Akita Fudoki'' * ''Gyōson Shiryaku'' * “Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi”<ref name="hinai">『大館郷土博物館研究紀要 火内』 Vol.12, March 2015, pp.13–29, “Materials on Matsumine-san Faith,” from the Matsumine-san Shinkō Iseki-gun Examination Subcommittee of the Ōdate City Cultural Property Protection Council</ref>
Other notable features on Matsumine-san include: * '''Haragawa''' – A small stream flowing from the waterfall of Fudō located on the right side below the stone steps of the approach. The waterfall is so named because it is used to wash away impurities from worshipers. ({{Coord|40|18|43.02|N|140|32|48.01|E|}}) * '''Shinmeisha''' – A small shrine on a hill about one chō (approximately 100 m) from the foot of the mountain; also called O-Ise-sama. ({{Coord|40|18|50.71|N|140|32|31.59|E|}}) * '''Yuden-yama''' – A distant monument to Yuden-yama, established in [[:en:1770|1770 AD]]. ({{Coord|40|18|48.76|N|140|32|35.53|E|}}) * '''Kōshin-zuka''' – A mound established in [[:en:1778|1778 AD]]. ({{Coord|40|18|48.61|N|140|32|34.72|E|}}) * '''Okoishi and Obaishi''' – Stones enshrining [[:en:Manjushri|Manjushri]] and [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Fugen Bosatsu]]. ({{Coord|40|18|54.11|N|140|32|20.70|E|}}) and ({{Coord|40|18|54.73|N|140|32|19.62|E|}}) * '''Yenaki Iwa''' – A stone said to have the power to silence a crying child. ({{Coord|40|18|54.42|N|140|32|10.97|E|}}) * '''Usa Shrine''' – A small shrine near the first torii where a small grass sickle is offered to cure smallpox in children. ({{Coord|40|18|53.77|N|140|32|04.32|E|}}) * '''The First Torii''' – A large stone torii; historically, a pond and garden existed to its right. ({{Coord|40|18|54.02|N|140|31|59.77|E|}}) * '''Denjuin''' – As recorded by Sugae Masumi, an illustration depicts Denjuin to the left of the first torii. This structure once existed between the first torii and the former pond and is said to mark the beginning of the mountain climbing route.<ref name="meisyo">“Matsumine Mountain Scenic Tour Association” (record, June 16, Heisei 3) by the Matsumine Town Association</ref> * '''Cedar Alley''' – A row of giant cedars between the first torii and the main shrine building. Although not mentioned in Sugae Masumi’s writings, old maps clearly depict it. Currently, the largest cedar is approximately 6.5 m in circumference and is over 600 years old. ({{Coord|40|18|53.18|N|140|31|56.64|E|}}) * '''Stone Steps''' – Approximately 170 stone steps (commonly stated as 160), also known as “Ishinokizahashi.”<ref name="matu"/> * '''Fudō-no-Taki''' – The waterfall of Fudō on the right side of the stone steps, whose water flows from a sheer cliff and eventually becomes Haragawa. Worshipers use it for purification before ascending to the main shrine. ({{Coord|40|18|52.91|N|140|31|53.66|E|}}) * '''Uga Shrine''' – A small stone shrine located to the right, along the waterfall’s flow, known as Uga no Kami; it is also called the small water shrine of Uga. ({{Coord|40|18|52.91|N|140|31|53.66|E|}}) * '''Main Shrine Building''' – The shrine grounds cover an area of 6 tan 11 bu, and the current main building was constructed by Satake Yoshinori starting in Meiji 3 and completed in April of Meiji 4. ({{Coord|40|18|52.23|N|140|31|50.23|E|}}) * '''Yakushidō''' – Located to the upper left of the main shrine building, also known as Hisu Shrine; dedicated to Yakushi Nyorai. ({{Coord|40|18|51.39|N|140|31|50.11|E|}}) * '''Yama Shrine''' – A small shrine dedicated to the mountain deity located to the right of the main building; proceeding around it leads to the source of Fudō-no-Taki. ({{Coord|40|18|52.87|N|140|31|50.84|E|}}) * '''Iwaya Jūimen Kannon''' – From the middle of the Cedar Alley, a side path leads to a large rock cave at the foot of the mountain, enshrining the Eleven-Faced Kannon. ({{Coord|40|18|50.03|N|140|31|57.18|E|}}) * '''Shiroiwa''' – A sheer white rock cliff to the left of the cave. * '''Tenjin no Iwa''' – A rock on the northern peak where ancient pines and other trees grow, known as Tenjin Rock. * '''Higashi Nozoki Iwa (Eastern Lookout Rock)''' – A massive rock jutting out to provide a view of the eastern sky. ({{Coord|40|18|59.12|N|140|31|46.83|E|}}) * '''Kagami Iwa''' – A rock that stands like a mirror; also referred to as Eboshi Iwa, due to its unusual shape. ({{Coord|40|18|59.18|N|140|31|46.67|E|}}) * '''Tainai Kugu (Inner Womb Cave)''' – A cave-like opening in the rock, said to evoke the feeling of being within a mother’s womb. ({{Coord|40|18|59.08|N|140|31|46.21|E|}}) * '''Hokoku Iwa''' – Located north of Tainai Kugu near the resting area; recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Nozoki Iwa” or “Byōbu Iwa,” where a “nozoki shugyō” similar to that of Ōmine-san was practiced. ({{Coord|40|18|59.58|N|140|31|43.35|E|}}) * '''Kyūjō''' – Near the summit, a slightly flat resting area where a triangular survey marker once stood. * '''Kineiwa''' – To the west of the resting area, a rock resembling a mortar carried by a moon rabbit. (Currently obscured by trees; on the western slope.) * '''Okunoin''' – Stairs on the western side of the resting area leading to an inner sanctuary called Okunoin (recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Oku no Goza”). From here, ancient features such as the Goma steps, a Zazen stone, and the rock of Gongen were once noted, though they are no longer identifiable. * '''Suzuri Iwa''' – Descending from the summit toward the south, a rock with a concave bottom that always contains water, known as Kōbō’s inkstone. (Near Ōiwa on a neighboring southeastern peak; now obscured by vegetation.) * '''Kengami Mine''' – A sharp rock outcrop with little foothold, described by Sugae Masumi as “Kengamine.” ({{Coord|40|18|42.71|N|140|31|49.76|E|}}) * '''Tengu Iwa''' – The large rocks on Kengami Mine are called Tengu Rock, with the larger one known as Great Tengu and the smaller as Little Tengu. (As recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Daitengu, Shōtengu no Iwa”.) * '''Hasami Iwa''' – Rocks facing each other resembling scissors; encountered along a small, relatively flat path obstructed by a large rock. ({{Coord|40|18|39.93|N|140|31|49.45|E|}}) * '''Tengu-bashi''' – Also known as the Tengu Suspension Bridge, it is the most scenic spot on the mountain. A massive rock bridges a deep chasm; crossing it offers a daunting view below. (Recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Daitengu no Tsuri-bashi.”) ({{Coord|40|18|37.95|N|140|31|51.35|E|}}) * '''Tsuzumi Iwa''' – A flat rock encountered when descending from Tengu Iwa, which produces a drum-like sound when stepped upon. (Recorded by Sugae Masumi as “Kago Iwa” and also as Tsuzumi Iwa.) ({{Coord|40|18|34.86|N|140|31|51.11|E|}}) After descending from Tsuzumi Iwa and turning left, one emerges below the First Torii and reaches the original road.<ref>『釈迦内郷土誌』, Shakani Kominkan, pp.265–269, composed during the Taishō era and reprinted in Heisei 1.</ref> == Sankokuga (Three-hooked Bell) == Sankokuga is an ancient bell excavated from Matsumine-san, which was presented to the Satake clan during the Edo period and is now housed in the [[:en:Tokyo National Museum|Tokyo National Museum]]. A receipt document from the Satake clan is recorded in the "Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi," and the "Hu Yin Onko-shi" confirms its existence. Locally, it is known as the "Station Bell" (Ekiro no Suzu). When [[Hitomi Shōu]] visited the region in 1797 (Kansei 9), he remarked that he had only heard of the Station Bell, and later Nikaidō Shokushima, in 1800 (Kansei 12), witnessed it and noted that it was housed at Seitōin in Kashima District or belonged to Matsumine-san in Dewa Akita-gun. He mentioned that it was unearthed in Tanaka about 100 years ago, and an elderly man from western regions confirmed that it was essentially identical to the bell from Kashima, hence the name "Station Bell" became established.<ref name="hinai"/> There is also a scholarly paper titled "On the Ancient Bell Housed by the Satake Family" discussing its true nature, though no definitive conclusion has been reached. This bell was transferred from the Satake family between April 24 and May 16, 1999 (Heisei 11) to the Tokyo National Museum, and was exhibited in the "Sankokuga Homecoming Exhibition" at the Ōdate Local Museum. According to some records in the "Kubota-gun Eki-ki," "Akita Fudoki," and "Gyōson Shiryaku," the bell was buried due to an earthquake, and an iron alligator was also excavated alongside it.<ref name="hinai"/> == Denjuin == Denjuin is recorded as the local temple of Matsumine-san. Sugae Masumi left an illustration of Denjuin, depicting it to the left of the First Torii when viewed from the base of the mountain. By the time the "Dewa Akita-gun Hinai-shō Matsumine-san Engi" was compiled, Denjuin had already been abolished. In [[:en:1598|1598 AD]], when the Asari clan perished and Ōdate came under the control of Akita Miki, Denjuin received a total of 70 shaku from the Akita clan. This indicates that Matsumine-san had been widely venerated in the Hinai region since the Asari era or earlier, independent of the Asari clan. During the Edo period, documents record that the Satake clan of Ōdate provided 9 shaku and two retinues.<ref name="hinai"/> == Fudō-dō == Fudō-dō is the main shrine building of Matsumine-san. According to records in the "Kubota-gun Eki-ki," "Akita Fudoki," and "Gyōson Shiryaku," it burned down in [[:en:1786|1786 AD]] (Tenmei 6). According to a document titled "Shoshokurichū-chō," Fudō-dō also burned down on the night of April 8, 1863 (Bunkyū 3) due to a fire, resulting in the loss of the Fudō statue, and the local Denjuin was ordered by the Satake clan to observe 50 days of mourning. Fudō-dō was reconstructed in [[:en:1867|1867 AD]] (Keiō 3). Timber was felled from within Matsumine-san, and contributions were solicited from the surrounding area. However, in 1868 (Keiō 4, Meiji 1), during the Akita War when Ōdate City was burned and amid the anti-Buddhist ([[:en:Haibutsu kishaku|Haibutsu kishaku]]) movement, although contributions of 180 ryo were collected at the time of reconstruction, by the time of the Fudō-dō relocation in 1871 only 1 ryo 2 bu was raised, indicating severe economic hardship.<ref name="hinai"/> Once a [[:en:Shingon Buddhism|Shingon sect]] temple known as Matsumine-san, it was later converted to a shrine in accordance with the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, with the principal deity changed to {{ill|Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|lt=Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|lt=Tsukuyomi|ja|月夜見命|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuyomi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ツクヨミ}}, and the name was changed to Matsumine Shrine. == Yakushi Shrine == Yakushi Shrine, also known as Hisu Shrine, is located on a small rise to the left of the main shrine building. It enshrines two statues of Yakushi Nyorai, which were donated in the Shōho Besshoku year (【1646 AD】) and in the Hōreki 10th year (【1760 AD】). In addition, many small stones with holes or inscribed with “me” are offered. A spring known as "Yakusui" is found midway up the steps; it is customary to purify one’s eyes with this water.<ref name="matu"/> == Tengu-sama == Among the many giant cedar and pine trees on Matsumine-san, one particularly distinctive giant cedar, known locally as the "Tengu Cedar," was reputed to have a hollow interior that served as the dwelling of tengu. However, as the tree died, it was cut down in Taishō 6, and the felled trunk was donated to Matsumine Shrine as a memorial. It is estimated to have had a diameter of nearly 3 m. During the Pacific War, families of soldiers—especially those whose relatives served in aviation units—visited the shrine and offered white and red paper fans in the hope of emulating the tengu’s ability to fly freely. It was also widely visited by families for protection against enemy bullets, due to the tengu’s reputed supernatural powers.<ref name="matu"/> == Suijin Shrine == Suijin Shrine is a small stone shrine located to the right, just before the stone steps. Known as Wakami, it is said that drinking water from here will restore youth; this tradition continues today on New Year’s Day.<ref name="matu"/> == Gosai == Gosai is a commemorative monument located to the left of the stone steps. There are no other monuments of its kind in Akita Prefecture. It is attributed to Emperor Uda. ({{Coord|40|18|51.82|N|140|31|51.31|E|}}) == Inari Shrine == The village shrine (satoyama) of Matsumine Shrine is an Inari Shrine, currently located in the western part of the Matsumine settlement ({{Coord|40|18|25.3|N|140|32|47.27|E|}}). Its enshrined deities are {{ill|Kura Inadama no Mikoto|ja|倉稲魂神|1=Ukanomitama|2=ja|3=倉稲魂神|4=de|5=Ukanomitama|6=eo|7=Ukanomitama|8=mni|9=ꯎꯀꯅꯣꯃꯤꯇꯃ|10=ru|11=Ука-но_митама|12=simple|13=Ukanomitama|14=sv|15=Ukanomitama|16=zh|17=宇迦之御魂神|lt=Ukanomitama|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kura Inadama no Mikoto|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ウカノミタマ}}, {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|lt=Sarutahiko Ōkami|lt=Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to サルタヒコ}}, and {{ill|Ōmiya-uru no Mikoto|ja|大宮売命|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōmiya-uru no Mikoto|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to オオミヤノメ|1=Ōmiyanome|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24865597}}. Its festival is held every October 10. Within its precincts there are monuments such as a stele of Sarutahiko, a “Twenty-Three Night Stele” (also known as Tsukimai-to), and a stone monument featuring a horse head.<ref name="matu"/> At the Inari Shrine, there are three dolls made of straw and pampas grass, with a history of approximately 450 years. Every last Sunday in November, the Matsumine settlement holds a doll festival. According to tradition, about 800 years ago, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshitsune|Minamoto no Yoshitsune]], accompanied by [[:en:Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] and [[:en:Nasu no Yoichi|Nasu no Yoichi]], passed through this area, inspiring the local people to create dolls out of reverence. These dolls were originally placed at the three entrances to the settlement to ward off epidemics and evil spirits, and were later enshrined within the Inari Shrine during the early Taishō period.<ref>「広報おおだて」, Shōwa 61, April 16</ref> == Records by Sugae Masumi and the Matumine-san Faith Sites == In June 1803 (Kyōwa 3), Sugae Masumi visited Matsumine-san and recorded his impressions in "Nie Nō Jikagarami." He noted, "On April 8, when a ceremony is held, many people come to worship at the main shrine. In the old days, those local Upase people who had not yet ascended to Nara’s Ōmine or Katsuragi would chant 'sange sange' and adorn themselves with prayer beads, bells, headscarves, and ayahikasa, carrying a dango-staff along with a spiral staff and a scepter, as they entered this peak." == Yamada Keizō == Marathon runner Yamada Keizō, from Ōdate City, who won the Boston Marathon in 1953 with a world record time, practiced running up and down the stone steps of Matsumine Shrine in his youth.<ref>Ōdate City, “Shakani Fieldwork – Matsumine Shrine Edition” [https://common3.pref.akita.lg.jp/genkimura/blog/?p=45876]</ref> == Matsumine Settlement and Matsumine Mine == The Matsumine Settlement, formerly known as Tanaka Village, was located at the confluence of the Shimonakagawa and Hanaokagawa rivers, about 300 m from the village. In 1963, a black ore deposit extending approximately 3000 mt was discovered 250–300 m underground beneath the settlement. Due to mining, subsidence occurred, and by 1976, 85 households were collectively relocated to the present site. In 1973, Matsumine Station was opened in the vicinity. Matsumine Mine extracted black ore from the Ōyama ore deposit using an open-column (open-pit) method. In 1932, its annual output surpassed that of the Ashio Copper Mine, and in 1970 it achieved a national record of 16,285 t per year. In 1979, despite aging facilities and maintenance expenses, soaring metal prices led to high revenues of 2.28 billion yen. However, due to a downturn in metal prices, the mine was closed in 1994 (Heisei 6), while leaving some reserves intact. During the Taishō period, this area suffered from severe smog caused by emissions from Kosaka Mine and Hanaoka Mine; the Matsumine area was the worst affected. Matsumine-san suffered greatly, with all its pine and chestnut trees dying, and in 1915 (Taishō 4) the entire mountain was deforested, leading to extensive reforestation. The history of this event is detailed on a commemorative monument by the shrine's stone steps.<ref name="matu"/> == Ōyama == {{Infobox mountain |Name = Ōyama |image = [[File:Ôyama(Ôdate si).jpg|250px]] |image Caption = Ōyama in Ōdate City (Matsumine-san) |Elevation = 375.6 m |Coordinates = {{coord|40|18|52.9|N|140|31|43.2|E|type:mountain_region:JP|display=inline}} |Location = {{JPN}}<br />[[:en:Akita Prefecture|Akita Prefecture]], [[:en:Ōdate|Ōdate City]], Matsumine Ōyama |Mountain Range = |Type = |First Ascent = |Map = {{Location map|Japan Akita Prefecture#Japan|relief=1|float=center}}{{日本の位置情報|40|18|53.05|140|31|43.2|Ōyama|40.314737,140.528669|Ōyama|nocoord=yes}} }} The highest peak of Matsumine-san is Ōyama (375.7 m), which epitomizes the very notion of a "mountain." On Ōyama, there is a pine known as the "Makka Pine," which, upon reaching 62 years of age, is said to be designated as such. Additionally, unusually for a mountain of roughly 300 m class, about 100 native [[:en:Fagus crenata|Buna]] trees grow here<ref name="matu"/>. Although the number of trees is small, Ōyama is home to many rare and endangered plant species, including [[:en:Arisaema thunbergii subsp. urashima|Urashima-sō]], [[:en:Cephalanthera erecta|Ginran]], {{ill|Ruiyōbotan|ja|ルイヨウボタン|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ruiyōbotan|qq=|1=Caulophyllum robustum|comment=changed title based on
